passages.text: Screening and in silico evaluation of candidate late-stage antigens for incorporation into multi-stage and post-exposure vaccines against tuberculosis

A quarter of the world's population harbours latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis, yet current vaccines, including BCG, offer limited protection against latency or reactivation. Multi-stage or post-exposure vaccines targeting antigens expressed during these phases may mitigate TB burden. This review screens late-stage Mtb antigens, evaluating their antigenicity, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy, summarizes in silico analyses, and discusses challenges and examples of vaccine design, highlighting candidates for incorporation into next-generation TB vaccines.
Introduction

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the main cause of tuberculosis (TB) in humans, remains a serious global health threat. Mathematical modelling estimated that one-quarter of the world's population in 2014 was latently infected with Mtb. Reactivation of this clinically latent infection is responsible for a large proportion of active TB cases each year. This contributed to an estimated 10.7 million new cases of active TB disease and 1.2 million deaths worldwide in 2024 alone.

With the hope of decreasing the high incidence and mortality of TB, the past two decades have witnessed considerable efforts to develop improved drugs and vaccines against this infection. Given the continuing spread of multi-drug-resistant Mtb strains and insufficiency of treatment to interrupt transmission in highly TB-burdened populations, the development of more effective vaccines seems to be a method of choice for controlling the spread of TB.

The only licensed vaccine against TB available today is the live attenuated bacterium Mycobacterium bovis Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG). BCG is a prophylactic vaccine; it protects children against pulmonary, meningeal, and miliary TB for up to 10 years, but its efficacy declines with each subsequent year. Accordingly, BCG offers variable protective efficacy (0-78%) against pulmonary TB in adults. Indeed, BCG does not confer protection against post-exposure active and latent TB, nor does it prevent TB reactivation later in life. As a consequence, BCG and leading prophylactic TB vaccines currently in clinical trials (https://tbtrialtrack.who.int/#/) may necessitate several decades to result in the eradication of TB, as they are unlikely to be effective in individuals already latently infected with Mtb. Thus, an ideal vaccine should prevent the progression to TB disease following primary infection, reinfection and reactivation of latent infection.

Given the substantial reservoir of latent TB in humans which has the potential of reactivation at any point in an individual's life; the inefficiency of BCG against latent TB and its reactivation; the failure of anti-TB medications due to the continuing spread of multidrug-resistant, extensively drug-resistant strains and the emergence of totally drug-resistant Mtb strains; as well as the escalation of co-infection with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) which has contributed to further reactivation of dormant TB; there is a crucial need for novel TB vaccines that incorporate antigens from all the three stages of Mtb infection: early infection, latency/dormancy and reactivation. These antigens can be used for the design of multi-stage vaccines exploiting the advantage of immune protection against all the stages of the infection or in post-exposure vaccines aiming at elimination/containment of latent TB and prevention of its reactivation.
Late-stage antigens encoded by Mtb
Tuberculosis phases (early, latency/dormancy, resuscitation, and reactivation).

Mtb infection exists on a continuum, ranging from elimination to active, contagious TB disease, and the Mtb antigenic repertoire varies across these stages. Mtb is transmitted via aerosol and primarily infects the lungs. Following exposure, only a minority of individuals develop primary TB disease. Early-phase antigens, including major vaccine candidates such as Ag85A-C, ESAT-6, and CFP-10, are expressed during this stage. Most individuals, however, control infection in a clinically asymptomatic state termed latent TB. Latency/dormancy is characterized by the formation of a solid granuloma in the lung, composed of immune cells, such as macrophages, dendritic cells, and T cells. Within these granulomas, Mtb persists in a dormant state with reduced replication and metabolism, expressing antigens of the DosR regulon, the EHR, and starvation antigens. Resuscitation occurs when immune control weakens, allowing dormant bacilli to be reawakened by resuscitation-promoting factors (RpfA-E). Reactivation is marked by caseous or necrotic granulomas. The reactivated bacilli downregulate DosR antigens while upregulating genes involved in metal transport, RNA, DNA, and cell wall synthesis. The reactivated infection may remain confined to the lung, leading to pulmonary TB, or disseminate to other organs. Secondary TB may also result from re-infection, instead of reactivation of latent infection. Mtb Mycobacterium tuberculosis, ESAT-6 early secreted antigenic target 6 kDa, CFP-10: culture filtrate protein 10 kDa, EHR enduring hypoxic response.

Tuberculosis progresses through four distinct phases: 1. Exposure: usually through inhaling airborne droplets of Mtb from a patient with active TB; 2. Primary infection: Mtb colonizes in the lung, and the immune system attempts to contain the infection by forming multi-layer structures of immune cells named granulomas; 3. Latent TB: the immune system succeeds in containing the infection, the bacilli remain dormant without causing symptoms, and are not transmissible; 4. Reactivation: the immune system might weaken due to factors such as aging, HIV infection, malnutrition, diabetes, or immunosuppressive medications, allowing the bacteria to begin multiplication and release from necrotic granulomas. This leads to the onset of active TB disease. Active TB, either from recent infection or reactivation, results in contagious spread of the pathogen. The antigenic repertoire of Mtb undergoes dynamic changes as the bacteria transition from primary infection to latency/dormancy and, ultimately, reactivation (Fig. 1).

Late-stage antigens of Mtb are expressed during the two phases of latency/dormancy and reactivation. In the latent phase, the highly expressed Mtb genes primarily belong to three groups: (i) The 48-gene dormancy regulon controlled by DosR (Rv3133c), which exhibits upregulation at the beginning of exposure to hypoxic conditions, low-dose nitric oxide, carbon monoxide exposure, and during infection in gamma interferon (IFN)-gamma-activated macrophages. (ii) The enduring hypoxic response (EHR) system, comprising nearly 230 genes that are activated later during hypoxia, shows a substantial overlap with Mtb genes induced by nutrient deprivation, includes many genes of the DosR regulon, and may contain the machinery used to enter into and survive latency. (iii) Genes encoding starvation antigens that are upregulated by Mtb upon nutrient depletion and possibly contribute to long-term survival within the host.

Under conditions where the host's immune protection is suppressed, the latent phase transitions towards reactivation. Induced by five resuscitation-promoting factors (Rv0867c, Rv1009, Rv1884c, Rv2389c and Rv2450c, named RpfA-E), resuscitation is characterized by the upregulation of a set of 174 genes. The five Rpfs are probably secreted or membrane-anchored, making them prospective targets for recognition by the host immune system. Consequently, they may be involved in inducing (protective) immune responses against TB reactivation.

During the reactivation phase, the recovery of cellular physiological and metabolic functions leads to the resumption of cell replication. The reactivation phase involves the downregulation of latency-associated genes, including DosR. On the contrary, genes involved in metal transport and remobilization, second messenger-mediated responses, DNA repair and recombination, and synthesis of major cell wall components are upregulated.

This review focuses on antigens associated with latency, resuscitation, and reactivation in Mtb, hereafter referred to as late-stage antigens. Figure 1 and Table 1 represent antigens that belong to each of these three stages.
The inefficiency of BCG in eliciting immune responses against late-stage antigens of Mtb

BCG is derived from an attenuated M. bovis strain, generated through repeated passaging of a virulent parent strain. During the attenuation period (1908-1966), the genome of various BCG strains underwent up to 25 regions of deletion (RD) compared to parental M. bovis. Despite its attenuated virulence, BCG retains several immune-evasion-associated constituents that may confer decoy immune reactions. This has been proposed as a potential contributor to BCG's limited efficacy in preventing reactivation of latent infection and may even condition the host for reactivation.

As a result of attenuation, BCG strains have also lost several immunologically essential components, including key T cell epitopes present in natural Mtb strains. For instance, early secreted antigenic target 6 kDa (ESAT-6) and culture filtrate protein 10 kDa (CFP-10), antigens included in some new TB vaccines, are encoded by RD1 and are absent in BCG. While certain regions have been lost, the DosR regulon retains over 97% amino acid sequence homology between BCG and Mtb, indicating 85.4% identicalness. Furthermore, RNA microarray analysis of 14 distinct BCG strains, following in vitro stimulation with hypoxia and exposure to nitric oxide, revealed a functional DosR regulon with an expression profile similar to that of Mtb. Despite these similarities, various studies have reported the failure of BCG vaccination to induce substantial immune responses to latency antigens. Vekemans et al. showed that neonatal BCG vaccination induced IFN-gamma responses to several non-DosR encoded antigens from Mtb, but not the DosR antigen HspX (Rv2031c). Lin et al. assessed immune responses to a series of TB latency antigens following vaccination with BCG, and reported that BCG vaccination did not increase the responses to these antigens, either in adolescent humans or in BALB/c mice. In contrast, responses to the latency antigens were observed in the mice vaccinated with plasmid DNAs encoding these proteins. Geluk et al. reported IFN-gamma responses to HspX were significantly higher in Mtb-exposed individuals compared to Mtb-unexposed BCG vaccinees. These results were further corroborated in HLA-DR3 and HLA-A2 transgenic mice, leading to the identification of two novel HspX-specific T cell epitopes. T cell responses against these HspX-derived epitopes were absent after BCG vaccination, whereas non-latency antigens were efficiently recognized.

Several other studies have substantiated the immunogenicity of both latency and resuscitation-associated antigens of Mtb (discussed in detail below). Therefore, the poor immune response to these antigens following BCG vaccination can largely be attributed to BCG's inability to express them. Indeed, BCG strains are unlikely to persist for prolonged periods in immunocompetent individuals, as they are rapidly controlled by the host immune response following vaccination. Thus, the late-stage gene products are unlikely to be induced after BCG vaccination. As a result, BCG fails to generate adequate immune responses to Mtb late-stage antigens and does not protect against the establishment of latent TB and its subsequent reactivation. That being the case, the immune responses to these antigens can be harnessed to complement BCG, boost immunity when administered after BCG priming, or enhance next-generation vaccines intended to replace BCG. To this aim, a more thorough understanding of immune responses to late-stage Mtb antigens will aid in identifying specific antigens contributing to protection against TB.
Impact of environmental mycobacteria sensitization on BCG efficacy

BCG efficacy against TB can be influenced by prior exposure to environmental mycobacteria. Studies have indicated that excluding infants and children already sensitized to mycobacteria was associated with a higher efficiency of BCG vaccination. In other words, BCG vaccination is more effective in infants and children who have not been previously sensitized to mycobacteria. Two main hypotheses explain this phenomenon. The masking hypothesis proposes that prior exposure to environmental mycobacteria provides baseline immunity that masks the additional protective effect of BCG. In contrast, the blocking hypothesis suggests that pre-existing exposure to environmental mycobacteria blocks BCG replication, preventing the vaccine from eliciting a strong protective immune response. These two hypotheses are not mutually exclusive and may occur simultaneously (for further discussion on these hypotheses, please refer to ref. ). Taken together, these observations support the development of vaccines as alternatives to BCG, specifically designed for administration to individuals with prior mycobacterial sensitization.
Heterologous protective benefits of BCG against non-TB infections

Among various vaccine approaches against TB (as reviewed by Zhuang et al. ), BCG presents a unique advantage. It has been suggested that BCG vaccination provides nonspecific (heterologous) protection in children, reducing morbidity and mortality caused by unrelated infections. A study conducted in Spain compared non-BCG-vaccinated children to those vaccinated at birth, and revealed that BCG vaccination was correlated with lower hospitalization rates due to non-TB-related respiratory infection and sepsis. Similarly, a study in Uganda compared infants vaccinated with BCG at birth or at 6 weeks of age, and found that within the first 6 weeks of life (before the latter group received BCG), infants who received BCG at birth showed a lower incidence of non-TB infections. A meta-analysis of 16 randomized controlled trials found that BCG vaccination offers an estimated 44% decrease in risk for non-TB respiratory infections and lowers all-cause mortality by 22% within one year of vaccination.

The heterologous protection conferred by BCG is linked to trained innate immunity, which involves epigenetic reprogramming of innate immune cells. Studies in mouse and human have shown that BCG vaccination trains bone marrow progenitors, circulating monocytes, macrophages and natural killer (NK) cells, and induces emergency granulopoiesis. Mechanistically, parenteral BCG can disseminate to gut-associated sites, inducing intestinal permeability leading to metabolomic changes in the gut, circulation and lungs. Specific metabolites, such as deoxycarnitine and butyrate, released into circulation following vaccination, modulate alveolar macrophages and enhance their protective response against subsequent Mtb infection. It is further shown that increased lactate levels in BCG vaccinated individuals lead to histone lactylation in monocytes and macrophages, contributing to trained immunity. BCG-induced trained innate immunity has shown beneficial effects across various diseases, including cancer, viral infections, and autoimmune diseases (please refer to ref. ). Whether prior Mtb infection or sensitization to environmental mycobacteria interferes with these heterologous benefits of BCG appears to be an interesting question for further investigation.

Given the heterologous protection offered by BCG, genetically modified BCG vaccines capable of inducing enhanced immune responses to antigens of latency and reactivation phases of TB represent promising candidates for multi-stage or post-exposure vaccines. Notably, significant protection against sustained, de novo Mtb infection was observed in South African adolescents after BCG revaccination. This being so, the overexpression of late-stage Mtb antigens by recombinant BCG (rBCG) vaccines can enhance the antigenic repertoire of the parental vaccine. Such modifications can extend beyond Mtb antigens and include antigens from co-infecting pathogens such as HIV, thereby contributing to the development of polyvalent multi-purpose rBCG vaccines.
Screening Mtb antigens for TB vaccine development based on infected human immune repertoires

Healthy individuals with a positive tuberculin skin test (TST), which uses purified protein derivative (PPD), or a positive interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA), such as QuantiFERON-TB Gold (QFT), which is based on Mtb-specific antigens ESAT-6 and CFP10, are classified as having latent TB infection and are referred to as latently Mtb-infected individuals (LTBI). Interpretation of these tests, however, must consider prior BCG vaccination and exposure to non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), both of which can cause false-positive TST results, with IGRA cross-reactivity reported in rare cases of NTM infection.

Healthy latently Mtb-infected individuals (H-LTBI) without active disease, such as healthy household contacts (HHC) of active pulmonary TB patients (PTB), are recognized to harbour protective immunity against TB. These subjects are extensively studied for identifying mycobacterial components suitable for vaccine development. Not only H-LTBI but also TB patients serve as reference populations for antigen screening. Indeed, models describing latent TB as a graded spectrum of infection suggest that even in individuals with active TB, immune responses capable of sterilizing at least some granulomas may exist. Consequently, the recognition of late-stage antigens by cells from TB patients is not unexpected. While such recognition can potentially reflect involvement of these antigens in TB pathogenesis, it may indicate a specific immune response directed against them.
Correlates of protection against TB.

IFN-gamma produced by Th1 cells stimulates infected macrophages to generate reactive nitrogen intermediates (RNI), promoting intracellular killing of bacteria (IKB). It also restricts the accumulation of terminally differentiated Th1 cells with poor parenchymal migration and enhances CD8+ T cells functions, including IFN-gamma and TNF production and lysis of infected macrophages. TNF-alpha is essential for macrophage RNI production. Th17 cells facilitate Th1 cells recruitment to the lung. IL-17 promotes T cells localization within lung lymphoid follicles (thereby activating macrophages), granuloma formation, IgA responses, and neutrophil recruitment. Neutrophils contribute antimicrobial peptides but can also drive immunopathology. Humoral immunity, including IgA against alpha-crystallin as well as anti-arabinomannan IgG and lipoarabinomannan-specific IgM, further enhances macrophage-mediated IKB. Collectively, balanced Th1/Th17 responses, together with antibody-mediated mechanisms, support effective innate immune activation and protection against TB. RNI reactive nitrogen intermediates, IKB intracellular killing of bacteria, TB tuberculosis, CTL cytotoxic T lymphocyte.

When screening sets of antigens for inclusion in TB vaccines, it is essential to compare the magnitude of positive responses between H-LTBI and TB patients to assess the protective value of each antigen. A higher frequency of cells recognizing an antigen in H-LTBI compared to TB patients indicates a greater likelihood that the immune response against this antigen contributes to infection control. Accordingly, several studies have reported a preferential recognition of Mtb late-stage antigens by peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from H-LTBI, and to a lesser extent, from TB patients. This suggests that the immune responses to these antigens may play protective roles against TB, potentially contributing to the control of latent Mtb infection and its subsequent reactivation. It should be further noted that this is a comparative approach used to prioritize antigens. The absolute immune response in TB patients may be influenced by the frequency, phenotype, and function of circulating T cells (discussed in detail below), which in turn affects their representation in PBMCs. Factors such as sequestration of T cells into infected tissues, lymphopenia, reduced proliferative capacity of T cells, and the progressive differentiation state of T cells in TB patients can modulate PBMCs' response in this population.
Correlates of protection against TB (Fig. 2)

While a complete understanding of protective immunity to Mtb is still lacking, research indicates that CD8+ and CD4+ lymphocytes, particularly CD4+ T-helper (Th)1 cells, play a key role in protection against TB. IFN-gamma produced by Th1 cells stimulates infected macrophages to generate reactive nitrogen intermediates, thereby restricting the growth of the intracellular Mtb. It is required for an effective CD8+ T cell response. These CD8+ T cells differentiate to cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) which in turn contribute to TB protection by producing IFN-gamma and TNF and by lysing infected macrophages. Th1 cell-derived IFN-gamma also limits the accumulation of terminally differentiated Th1 cells in the lung vasculature, which are unable to effectively migrate into the lung parenchyma. TNF-alpha is essential for reactive nitrogen production by macrophages. Research also points to the protective role of IL-17-producing CD4+ T cells (i.e., Th17 cells) and IL-17 in TB. Th17 cells mediate recruitment of IFN-gamma-producing CD4+ T cells to the lung to restrict Mtb growth. IL-17 mediates localization of T cells within lung lymphoid follicles, thereby activating macrophages and limiting Mtb growth. It also induces granuloma formation, and is required for the induction of immunoglobulin A (IgA) responses in the lung, which serve as a correlate of local protection. IL-17 and its receptor signalling are essential for neutrophil recruitment to the lungs, which contributes to innate resistance against TB via antimicrobial peptides. However, an excessive neutrophil response can cause immunopathology, highlighting the need for a regulated Th17 response.

Concerning humoral responses, in addition to IgA (e.g., against alpha-crystallin), monoclonal IgG against Mtb surface molecules such as arabinomannan, as well as lipoarabinomannan-specific IgM, have been shown to contribute to and correlate with protection, respectively. These antibodies can enhance the macrophage-mediated killing of intracellular Mtb, among other functions. Collectively, a balanced Th1/Th17 response that controls bacterial growth while limiting immunopathology appears to be a key correlate of protective immunity against TB, as observed in asymptomatic LTBI macaques, with antibody responses potentially contributing as well (Fig. 2). For an extended overview of the cells and mediators associated with TB protection, please refer to this book chapter (by Peralta Alvarez et al.).
Promiscuous antigens and safety of vaccines incorporating Mtb late-stage antigens

Given the broad heterogeneity in major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I and II alleles, selecting antigens for inclusion in a new TB vaccine necessitates epitopes that bind to a wide range of human leucocyte antigens (HLA), referred to as promiscuous epitopes. Indeed, to develop a vaccine that effectively protects genetically diverse human populations, promiscuous recognition of the candidate antigens by individuals of various ethnic backgrounds is vital. Certain Mtb antigens have been shown to elicit population-dependent responses due to genetic variations in host immune responses, variations in circulating Mtb strains, and differences in assays employed. However, numerous latency and resuscitation-associated antigens have consistently demonstrated recognition across diverse populations. These antigens emerge as promising candidates for incorporation into new TB vaccines (further discussed below).

Alongside the required promiscuous nature, late-stage antigens of Mtb must meet safety criteria for inclusion in multi-stage and particularly post-exposure TB vaccines. A post-exposure vaccine should induce protective immunity in individuals with pre-existing T cell responses to mycobacterial antigens that are persistent (in H-LTBI and HHC), waning (in household contacts with incipient disease), or absent (in patients successfully treated for TB). To ensure the success of this vaccination, the pre-existing immunity in the host and the vaccine-induced immunity must interact synergistically. If the vaccine-induced immunity counteracts the pre-existing immunity, it may trigger severe Koch-like reactions. The Koch reaction refers to the necrotic inflammation that occurs at the site of challenge in Mtb-infected guinea pigs following exposure to either live mycobacteria or mycobacterial antigens. Accordingly, Koch-like reactions in LTBI or cured patients can lead to tissue-destructive reactions, necrosis and bacterial dissemination.

Furthermore, there remains scepticism surrounding the incorporation of Rpfs into post-exposure vaccines, primarily due to the lack of conclusive evidence on whether such vaccines can sterilize latent lesions without reawakening the disease process. Thus, it is imperative to ensure the safety of a candidate vaccine harbouring Mtb late-stage antigens, particularly when intended for use in a post-exposure setting. Safety tests must be conducted in animal models of latent TB to confirm that the disease does not reactivate, nor is it exacerbated. Severe weight loss, an increased bacterial CFU in the lungs, or bacterial dissemination to other tissues are key indicators of disease progression and potential safety concerns in experimental models. For this purpose, macaques serve as a more suitable animal model, as small-animal models fail to reproduce key aspects of human latent infection.

When administering protein or subunit vaccines to animals for safety testing, the choice of adjuvant can significantly affect immunological outcomes. A study compared five different adjuvant:Alum, MF59 , GLA-SE, IC31  and CAF01:each formulated with a fusion of three Mtb antigens (Ag85B, ESAT-6 and Rv2660c), to assess immunogenicity and protective efficacy in mice. Each adjuvant induced a distinct immunological signature, characterized by varying levels of humoral (IgG1/IgG2a) and cellular (Th1/Th2/Th17) responses, highlighting the role of adjuvants in shaping immune responses. Similarly, formulation of mycobacterial antigen PPE15 with five different adjuvants produced differential IgG and T helper cells responses. These findings suggest that, when evaluating the safety of a candidate late-stage Mtb antigen in animal models, it is advisable to test the antigen in combination with different adjuvants.

While essential for safety testing, animal models have limitations due to species-specific differences in TB pathogenesis. Studying cytokine profiles after ex vivo stimulation of PBMCs from H-LTBI and TB patients can further help anticipate the safety of a candidate antigen. As discussed, immunity to Mtb infection requires a predominant Th1 response, with contributions from Th17 cells. If a candidate antigen stimulates Th2 cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-4, in preference to Th1 types, such as IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha, it is less likely to enforce post-exposure protection in LTBI. Instead, such a response may potentially compromise the existing immunity.
Schematic outlining recommended steps for selecting late-stage Mtb antigens for incorporation into novel multi-stage and post-exposure TB vaccines.

Candidate antigens should be broadly recognized across diverse human populations to ensure effectiveness across different HLA backgrounds (i.e., promiscuity). Safety evaluations, especially for post-exposure vaccines, are essential to minimize the risk of reactivation of latent TB infection and excessive reactogenicity in LTBI. For immunobiological studies, selected antigens should be evaluated for antigenicity in PBMCs or whole-blood cultures from LTBI and, to a lesser extent, active TB patients. Immunogenicity and protective efficacy should then be evaluated in relevant animal models and challenge studies. In silico analyses and computational tools should be used to further evaluate and prioritize antigens. Alignment with existing datasets and published studies can strengthen confidence in antigen selection. These steps may be carried out before or after immunobiological evaluations. Clinical trials remain the gold standard for confirming the safety, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy of TB vaccines incorporating selected late-stage antigens. Across phases I, II, and III, clinical trials establish optimal dosing, safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy in preventing IGRA/QFT conversion or infection in uninfected individuals, as well as progression to bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB disease in LTBI. Upon passing the promiscuousness and safety consideration steps, candidate antigens can undergo further screening (discussed below) to ascertain their suitability as pertinent vaccine candidates (Fig. 3).
Antigenicity versus immunogenicity and protective efficacy of the candidate antigens

Identifying, isolating, and immunobiologically characterizing the mycobacterial components involved in eliciting protective immune responses are critical steps in screening vaccine candidates against TB. However, due to the absence of validated correlates of protection and the unavailability of a human challenge model, selecting antigens depends on their ability to be recognized by T cells from H-LTBI and subsequently induce IFN-gamma in ex vivo assays (referred to as antigenicity).

To establish a causal link between the observed T cell responses in LTBI and their protection against TB, it is essential to conduct follow-up studies on untreated H-LTBI who continue to control Mtb infection over the long term and remain healthy. Specifically, monitoring the association between IFN-gamma responses to late-stage antigens in H-LTBI and long-term protection against TB disease is crucial. Of interest, higher IFN-gamma/IL-10 ratios were shown to correlate with protection after natural TB exposure; HHC showed elevated IFN-gamma/IL-10 ratios compared to the household contacts who contracted TB. These factors should be considered when evaluating the antigenicity of candidate antigens.

In addition to, or as an alternative to, antigenicity, assessing the immunogenicity of a vaccine candidate is crucial. This involves evaluating the antigens' in vivo activity in immunized animal models, followed by ex vivo stimulation of the T cells to study cytokine profiles.

A vaccine candidate, demonstrating antigenicity and immunogenicity, may warrant evaluation for protective efficacy in animal models challenged with Mtb. An antigen is considered protective if vaccinated animals exhibit a reduction of more than 0.3 log10 in pathogen load following the challenge, compared to unvaccinated controls. Protection against experimentally induced reactivation of latent infection should also be tested, although such studies have been rarely conducted to date.

Notably, certain antigens have shown antigenicity and immunogenicity with protective activity in animal models, but these results did not consistently translate to significant immune responses and/or protection in humans, as discussed later. Hence, there is no certainty in extrapolating results from animal models to humans, with one possible reason being the differences observed in disease progression. This highlights the importance of clinical trials. Clinical trials serve as the gold standard for assessing the protective value of a vaccine candidate (Fig. 3).

In the upcoming section, an overview of existing studies investigating Mtb late-stage antigens is provided. These studies delve into the antigenicity of these antigens across diverse ethnic groups, explore their immunogenicity, and address their protective potential using animal models. A list of the top 10 antigens is extracted from each of these studies and is presented in Table 1.
Overview of studies assessing antigenicity, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy of Mtb late-stage antigens

In a study conducted by Leyten et al., 25 DosR regulon-encoded proteins underwent evaluation. The study utilized proliferation assays and measurement of IFN-gamma responses in 12 Mtb-specific T cell lines and PBMCs. PBMCs were collected from TB patients, H-LTBI who had not developed active TB over a mean period of 5.5 years, and healthy controls (HC), predominantly of Dutch origin. The results indicated that all of the 25 latency antigens induced the production of IFN-gamma in at least one T cell line, and 18 were also recognized by PBMCs from at least 10% of either TB patients or H-LTBI. Notably, several of the DosR-encoded antigens, such as Rv1733c, Rv2029c, Rv2627c and Rv2628, elicited stronger IFN-gamma responses in H-LTBI compared to individuals with active TB. Interestingly, the magnitude of these responses was even higher than the TB patients' responses to the major early-phase antigen CFP-10. As discussed earlier, H-LTBI remained healthy for 5.5 years, and the stronger responses observed in H-LTBI compared to TB patients to these antigens suggest potential involvement in controlling the infection and indicate the possible protective value of these antigens.

In a subsequent study conducted by Roupie et al., plasmid DNA vaccination was administered to BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice. The study aimed to analyse the immunogenicity of eight DosR regulon-encoded antigens previously identified by Leyten et al. as strong stimulators of T cell responses in H-LTBI. Among these antigens, DNA encoding Rv2626c induced the highest level of IFN-gamma and IL-2 in splenocytes of both mouse strains, followed by Rv2031c, Rv2032, Rv2627c, Rv2628, Rv1733c, Rv1738 and Rv2029c, respectively. Stimulation of splenocytes from the DNA-vaccinated mice with overlapping peptide sets led to mapping several immunodominant epitopes for Rv2029c, Rv2031c, Rv2626c, Rv2627c, and Rv2628, yet none were identified for Rv1733c. BALB/c mice persistently infected with Mtb demonstrated significantly increased IFN-gamma levels in response to Rv2031c (33-fold), Rv1733c, and Rv2626c (fourfold), and Rv2029c (twofold) compared to acutely infected mice. This implies the potential of these antigens to be incorporated into post-exposure vaccines.

Lin and colleagues investigated the immune responses elicited by seven Mtb latency antigens in BCG-vaccinated adults, predominantly of Dutch origin. They categorized the subjects into two groups based on their likely exposure to Mtb, using IFN-gamma levels in response to major early-phase antigens ESAT-6 and/or CFP-10. Notably, Mtb-exposed vaccinees exhibited stronger IFN-gamma responses in PBMCs and a higher proportion of responders compared to the unexposed group for the seven studied antigens. Furthermore, vaccination of BALB/c mice with plasmids encoding these seven DosR antigens, along with the latency antigen Rv1738, induced robust T cell responses to six of these eight antigens. Among these antigens, Rv2626c elicited the highest IFN-gamma production upon ex vivo stimulation of splenocytes from the immunized mice, followed by Rv1733c, Rv2032, and Rv2031c, respectively.

Bertholet et al. employed computational analyses and selection criteria, including gene induction during growth in macrophages, up- or down-regulation under hypoxia and carbon limitation, involvement in encoding secreted/membrane-associated proteins, and/or being a member of the pathogenicity-associated membrane protein families PE/PPE or EsX. Their selection yielded 94 Mtb genes, with 49 proteins, including 10 hypoxia-associated proteins, that induced the highest IFN-gamma levels and the highest percentage of positive responders when tested with PBMCs from healthy PPD-positive individuals suspected of TB exposure. Notably, these 49 proteins did not stimulate responses in PBMCs from PPD-negative donors. This points to a TB-specific immune response by these antigens. These proteins were adjuvanted with CpG oligodeoxynucleotides and assessed for protective efficacy in C57BL/6 mice challenged with a low dose of Mtb H37Rv or Erdman strain. Among these, 12 proteins, exemplified by Rv1813c, induced decreases in lung CFU between 0.1 and 0.3 log10, while six antigens, such as Rv3044, elicited over 0.3 log10 reduction. It was further shown that protection in mice vaccinated with the highly protective antigens was associated with a Th1 immune response.

Another study involving German participants assessed 29 antigens related to latency, resuscitation, and reactivation of Mtb. Schuck and colleagues analysed the frequencies of IFN-gamma-expressing T cells and the levels of IFN-gamma production by PBMCs from H-LTBI, active PTB, and TST-negative donors. Through a 7-day ex vivo restimulation, these antigens were found to induce IFN-gamma in T cells from the majority of H-LTBI. Low to no responses were observed in TST-negative donors. Among these antigens, eleven elicited strong responses in the H-LTBI, with seven of them - including two reactivation antigens (Rv3407 and Rv0140), three DosR regulon-encoded antigens (Rv1733c, Rv2003c and Rv2005c), and two Rpfs (Rv1009 and Rv2450c)-induced significantly higher T cell responses in H-LTBI compared to PTB.

Black et al. conducted a screening involving seven classical Mtb antigens and 51 candidate antigens spanning the entire DosR regulon. They assessed the induction of IFN-gamma responses in seven-day whole blood cultures. Samples were obtained from HHC of PTB in three high-burden countries in Africa, including South Africa, The Gambia, and Uganda. The results indicated population-specific responses to some of the DosR regulon-encoded antigens. However, seven of these antigens were among the 10 most frequently recognized antigens in two or three countries. This points to the promiscuous potential of these seven antigens. These included Rv0081, Rv1733c, Rv1735c, Rv1736c-C terminal part, Rv1737c, Rv1997-C terminal part and Rv2006. Notably, Rv1733c was the most commonly recognized antigen in both South Africa and Uganda, and it ranked third in The Gambia. In contrast, HspX (Rv2031c) did not rank among the top antigens in any of these three countries.

Chegou et al. investigated 118 diverse Mtb infection-phase-dependent antigens, which included eight well-characterized TB antigens, 51 DosR-induced, 23 reactivation, six starvation, five Rpfs, and 24 stress-associated antigens. The antigens were evaluated for their ability to induce IFN-gamma in a 7-day whole blood culture from PTB and HHC of PTB in a high TB burden setting in South Africa. The results showed that the DosR regulon-encoded antigens were more frequently recognized by HHC than PTB, and the differences in IFN-gamma responses were significant for 14 out of the 51 studied antigens. Interestingly, all five Rpfs induced significantly higher IFN-gamma responses in HHC than in PTB. This points to the likely involvement of these antigens in protection against TB. However, the IFN-gamma levels elicited by most of the TB reactivation antigens, starvation, and stress-associated antigens were generally low in both PTB and HHC groups, with no significant difference observed.

Riano and colleagues screened a panel comprising five Rpfs, 18 DosR-encoded, and five stress-induced antigens using 7-day ex vivo restimulation of PBMCs. The study participants included HHC latently infected with Mtb (LTBI-HHC) of Colombian origin who had remained healthy for over 3 years. The study identified three DosR-encoded antigens (Rv1737c, Rv2029c and Rv2628c) and two Rpfs (Rv0867c and Rv2389c) as the most potent IFN-gamma-inducing antigens in these LTBI-HHC. The findings indicated significant increases in the frequency of CD4+IFN-gamma+ T cells in response to the three selected DosR antigens and to Rv2389c, but not Rv0867c, in LTBI-HHC compared to PTB. Distinctive patterns of cytokine and chemokine induction by the selected DosR antigens and Rpfs were observed in PBMCs from LTBI-HHC and PTB. For instance, higher levels of IL-2 were induced by Rv2029c and Rv1737c in LTBI-HHC compared to PTB; Rv2628c induced higher levels of IL-10 in LTBI-HHC; while Rv2389c induced higher IL-10 levels in PTB.

Kassa et al. evaluated IFN-gamma responses using a 7-day whole blood assay among Ethiopian PTB. The study focused on screening a panel consisting of five classical and 64 non-classical antigens (39 DosR regulon-encoded, four Rpfs, and 21 reactivation antigens). Among the 64 non-classical antigens, 23 were identified as inducers of IFN-gamma responses. Notably, eight of these antigens were strong inducers of IFN-gamma, and 10 were recognized by most of the study participants. The Rpfs elicited the highest levels of IFN-gamma with the highest percentage of positive respondents compared to the latency and reactivation antigens. The study also reported distinct cytokine expression profiles in response to 29 antigens that were selected. Interestingly, the IL-10 response to most of the strong IFN-gamma inducers was low, indicating a high IFN-gamma to IL-10 ratio and likely involvement in protection. In contrast, the IL-10 response to Rv1009, Rv2389c and Rv2629 was high, indicating their possible involvement in the pathogenesis of TB.

In a study conducted by Derrick and colleagues, 16 recombinant TB proteins, including four DosR-encoded antigens previously identified as immunogenic in animal models, were tested. These purified proteins were formulated in dimethyl dioctadecyl ammonium bromide with trehalose 6,6 dibenenate adjuvant for evaluation of their protective efficacy. The study used C57BL/6 mice challenged with a low dose of Mtb Erdman. Vaccinated mice exhibited a reduction in lung CFU compared to non-vaccinated controls, with 0.3-0.5 log10 reductions for Rv1735c and Rv2032. However, the remaining two DosR antigens (Rv1733c and Rv2626c) did not induce significant pulmonary protection (<0.3 log10 reduction).

Sierra-Vidal and colleagues conducted a study using 18-hour and 7-day whole blood cultures to evaluate a panel of 60 antigens. These included six DosR regulon-encoded, 12 reactivation, one Rpf (Rv2389c), one starvation, six stress-associated, and 34 in vivo-expressed Mtb antigens. The participants included individuals without TB infection, LTBI, and subjects with active TB. The findings revealed the induction of IFN-gamma responses to two latency antigens (Rv1733c and Rv2627) and Rv2389c in cultures from LTBI. Notably, Rv1733c elicited the highest response in LTBI in both the 18-hour and 7-day assays. This heightened response in LTBI surpassed the responses observed in both non-infected individuals and TB patients, enabling differentiation among the three study groups. In contrast, the response induced by Rv2389c in LTBI was similar to that of the non-infected group but remained higher compared to TB patients.

In a study conducted by Yeremeev and colleagues, subunit vaccines of Rpf from Micrococcus luteus and the five mycobacterial Rpfs were administered to C57BL/6 mice. Lymph node cells from the immunized mice showed T cell proliferation, with the highest response observed after ex vivo stimulation with RpfB, followed by RpfA, RpfE, RpfD, and the micrococcal Rpf, respectively. RpfC induced the least proliferative response. Except for RpfC and RpfB, all studied Rpfs exhibited weak mitogen properties and cross-reactivity in T cell responses. Notably, RpfB, despite eliciting a high level of antigen-specific T cell response, showed neither mitogenicity nor cross-reactivity. When RpfA, RpfB, and RpfD were tested for cytokine production, higher levels of antigen-specific IFN-gamma were elicited, and low (RpfD) to moderate (RpfA and B) levels of IL-10 were observed compared to the micrococcal Rpf. Vaccination of mice with either RpfE or micrococcal Rpf conferred significant protection against high-dose Mtb H37Rv challenge, as demonstrated by log10 reductions of 2 and 1 in mycobacterial loads in lung and spleen, respectively, along with extended post-infection survival.
In silico analyses of the top candidate antigens

Although the evaluation of immunobiological properties (antigenicity, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy) of mycobacterial components has been instrumental in the identification of potential vaccine candidates, in silico analyses can serve as an effective tool for initial screening or, conversely, for reinforcing the selection of specific antigens as viable vaccine candidates. In this section, an overview of several publicly available databases suitable for computational characterization of Mtb antigens is provided. Based on the ranking derived from Table 1, key characteristics of the top 10 latency antigens (all DosR regulon-encoded) along with the four selected Rpfs are delineated (Table 2).

B-cell activation and differentiation into plasma cells are essential for generating a humoral immune response against an antigen. Continuous B-cell epitopes were predicted using BepiPred 2.0 (https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/services/BepiPred-2.0/) and ABCpred servers (http://crdd.osdd.net/raghava/abcpred/) using default threshold and parameters.

Antigenic epitopes presented onto MHC I and MHC II molecules can, respectively, activate CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, leading to cytotoxic and helper T cell responses. ProPred (http://crdd.osdd.net/raghava/propred/) was used to predict MHC class II binding regions. The analysis was carried out with a threshold of 1% (high stringency) for all 51 HLA-DR alleles available on the server. 15-mer CD4+ T cell epitopes with scores higher than 20 were determined for all the default types of MHC class II molecules on the SYFPEITHI server (http://www.syfpeithi.de/bin/MHCServer.dll/EpitopePrediction.htm). HLA class II and class I binding regions were predicted using the HLAPred server (http://crdd.osdd.net/raghava/hlapred/). All the alleles from the list of 54 HLA class I and 51 HLA class II were selected for the prediction of T cell epitopes using a threshold of 1% (the highest stringency). Interestingly, there was a complete agreement between the results obtained from ProPred and HLAPred regarding the number of MHC-II epitopes identified within the sequence of each antigen. Prediction of T cell epitopes restricted to 10 MHC class I supertypes was carried out by the use of NetCTL integrative approach (NetCTL-1.2) (https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/services/NetCTL-1.2/), applying the default threshold and parameters. Antigenicity (the ability of an antigen to be recognized by the immune system) and allergenic potential (the ability of a substance to trigger an allergic immune response in susceptible individuals) were determined for each protein by the VaxiJen V.2 server (https://www.ddg-pharmfac.net/vaxijen3/home/) and AlgPred server (http://crdd.osdd.net/raghava/algpred/), respectively.

Membrane-associated and secreted antigens are considered superior candidates for eliciting T cell responses due to their enhanced accessibility to the immune system. To identify these candidate antigens, SignalP (https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/services/SignalP-5.0/) was utilized to predict secretion via the SecA pathway, while TATfind (http://signalfind.org/tatfind.html) was employed to search for the twin-arginine translocation (Tat) motif associated with the TAT pathway. Additionally, the TBpred server (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/tbpred/submission.html) was used to predict subcellular localization of the candidate antigens.

Other information extracted from MycoBrowser portal includes the most probable cellular location of each antigen, and the number of predicted transmembrane helices using Hidden Markov Models. Among the highest-ranking antigens, one (Rv1997) was predicted to harbour 10 transmembrane domains. Consequently, this antigen was excluded from Table 2 due to the anticipated technical challenges associated with cloning and producing a recombinant protein of this nature.

Comparative genomic analyses indicate that late-stage antigens are not exclusively expressed by Mtb, and many species of NTM exhibit moderate to high degrees of sequence homology in genes encoding these antigens. Such homology can result in cross-reactivity between Mtb and NTM antigens, posing a challenge for inclusion into live vaccines; As discussed previously, prior exposure to environmental mycobacteria has been documented to reduce the efficacy of BCG. Orthologs to each of our candidate antigens have been identified in various NTM species listed in Table 2. Careful considerations should be given to incorporating highly cross-reactive antigens into live vaccines, as they might diminish the vaccine efficacy, particularly in highly endemic populations.

Further to considering cross-reactivity, an antigen's suitability for incorporation into live or post-exposure vaccines may come into question if it is involved in immune evasion, pathogenesis, or virulence of Mtb. Notably, among our candidates, Rv2031c is predicted to have such functions.

Several bioinformatics-based studies have investigated the screening of mycobacterial components for incorporation into new TB vaccines. It is therefore beneficial to compare the antigens selected here with those identified in existing analyses. Accordingly, the final two rows of Table 2 present the rankings of each vaccine candidate based on the study by Zvi et al.. Additionally, the table represents antigens that were deemed pertinent vaccine candidates by Nguyen Thi and colleagues. The recurrence of specific antigens across these independent studies suggests their potential as strong vaccine candidates.
Challenges of incorporating late-stage antigens into multi-stage and post-exposure TB vaccines

As discussed earlier, multi-stage and post-exposure vaccines represent a promising approach in the fight against TB. Multi-stage vaccines target various infection phases (early, latent, and reactivation), providing comprehensive protection. Post-exposure vaccines aim to protect those already exposed to Mtb, particularly individuals with latent TB, by boosting immune responses to control or eliminate latent bacteria before they cause symptomatic disease. Developing effective post-exposure vaccines is crucial to curb transmission and prevent outbreaks in high-burden regions where latent TB is prevalent. Accordingly, compared with prophylactic and therapeutic approaches, post-exposure TB vaccines hold the greatest potential for rapid global health impact.

Incorporating Mtb late-stage antigens into multi-stage or post-exposure vaccines is conceptually appealing but introduces several challenges. A major concern is antigen stability to maintain vaccine effectiveness during thermal fluctuation, storage and transportation in low-resource settings. Notably, a lyophilized formulation of the adjuvanted subunit vaccine, ID93 + GLA-SE, has demonstrated enhanced thermal stability for at least three months when stored at 37  C and up to 24 months when stored at 5  C, while maintaining safety and immunogenicity.

Combining multiple antigens in a single vaccine can further complicate formulation and potentially dilute the immunogenicity of individual antigens; Antigenic interference may occur, whereby a highly immunogenic antigen suppresses immune responses to less immunogenic ones. This issue is particularly relevant for polyvalent multi-purpose vaccines targeting TB alongside co-infecting pathogens such as HIV. Such interference can diminish overall vaccine effectiveness by preventing balanced immune responses across all antigens. To address this, potent adjuvants and/or optimized delivery systems are needed to elicit robust and coordinated immunity.
Role and selection of adjuvants in TB vaccine development

In general, protein or peptide antigens in subunit vaccines are insufficiently immunogenic on their own and require adjuvants to elicit protective immunity. The term adjuvant is often used broadly to refer to both immune-stimulating agents and delivery systems. Selecting an appropriate adjuvant is crucial, as different adjuvants stimulate the immune system in distinct ways, and some may not induce adequate protective responses. Adjuvants enhance the efficiency and specificity of vaccine-induced immune responses through improving vaccine stability, prolonged retention and sustained release of antigen, lymph node targeting, acting as carriers to deliver antigens to antigen-presenting cells, prolonging antigen exposure, enhancing antigen presentation, and regulating innate immune cell activation. To effectively stimulate protection against TB, an adjuvant should elicit a strong cellular immune response, favouring Th1/Th17 pathways over Th2. Inducing humoral responses is beneficial but secondary.

Alum (aluminium hydroxide) is one of the most widely used adjuvants due to the profile of safety, stability and cost-effectivity. While it enhances the antibody response, it is associated with a major Th2-bias to the immune response. Indeed, a study in mice showed that alum failed to confer protection when used as an adjuvant in a subunit TB vaccine.

Lipid-based adjuvants, such as emulsions and liposomes, act as both adjuvants and delivery systems. Oil-in-water emulsions containing squalene oil, such as AS03 and MF59, are known to elicit antibody responses. They also induce a mixed Th1/Th2 response. Liposomes, such as liposome-based AS01, are effective adjuvant-delivery systems due to their high loading capacity, targetability, biocompatibility, ability to enhance antigen presentation, and tuneable features such as size and charge.

Most adjuvants currently in TB clinical trials are formulated to combine an immunomodulator that activates immune cells through pathogen-recognition receptors (PRRs), such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs), with a delivery system that enhances antigen targeting. Optimizing the ratio of these components is essential to maximize synergistic immunological benefits. An example of this two-component system is the TB adjuvant GLA-SE, which contains a synthetic TLR4 agonist, glucopyranosyl lipid A (GLA) formulated in an oil-in-water squalene emulsion. Another is AS01, which combines monophosphoryl lipid A (MPL, a TLR4 agonist) with QS-21, a highly purified saponin, co-formulated in liposomes. Two promising post-exposure TB vaccine candidates utilizing these adjuvants, ID93 + GLA-SE and M72/AS01_E, will be discussed in detail in the next section.

Dextran/CpG, the adjuvant used in GamTBvac, combines dextran 500 kDa and diethylaminoethyl (DEAE)-dextran 500 kDa with CpG oligodeoxynucleotides (TLR9 agonist). GamTBvac induced antigen-specific IFN-gamma and IgG responses in mice and conferred significant protection in Mtb-challenged mice and guinea pigs when administered as a BCG booster vaccine. In a phase II trial in BCG-vaccinated, uninfected healthy adults, GamTBvac was well tolerated and elicited Th1 cells producing various combinations of IFN-gamma, IL-2, and TNF-alpha, along with antigen-specific IgG responses. A phase III clinical trial is currently recruiting adults to evaluate the protective efficacy of the vaccine in preventing pulmonary TB (NCT04975737).

IC31  is the combination of the single-stranded DNA-phosphodiester oligo-d(IC)13 (ODN1a) and the antimicrobial peptide KLKL5KLK. It signals through TLR9 with induction of Th1/Th2, CTL and antibody responses in mice. IC31  has been tested with three different fusion proteins (H1, H4, H56) in various clinical trials. H56:IC31 will be discussed in detail in the following section.

Trehalose 6,6-dibehenate (TDB) is a synthetic analogue of the mycobacterial cord factor located in the bacterium cell wall. It activates murine macrophages via a C-type lectin receptor called Mincle, eliciting a Th1/Th17 response. TDB also engages human Mincle and stimulates monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells to produce a variety of cytokines. TDB, incorporated into dimethyldioctadecyl-ammonium (DDA) liposomes at a 1:5 weight ratio, forms CAF01. In a phase I clinical trial, escalating doses of CAF01 formulated with fusion protein H1 induced long-lived Th1 responses, persisting for 150 weeks. For a more detailed discussion on adjuvants in TB vaccines, please refer to the review by Zhang and colleagues.

In clinical trials, adjuvanted TB vaccines have demonstrated immunogenicity but are often reactogenic. For instance, in LTBI (IGRA-positive), the adjuvanted subunit vaccine M72/AS01_E was associated with a higher rate of unsolicited adverse events (~67% vs. ~45% with placebo). This was primarily due to injection site reactions and flu-like symptoms, although the incidence of serious adverse events was comparable between groups. ID93 + GLA-SE caused injection site erythema in 2 of 48 participants, and injection site pain was more frequent in ID93 + GLA-SE regimens than with ID93 alone. Additionally, mild injection site reactions and flu-like symptoms were more common in LTBI (QFT-positive) than in uninfected individuals. Notably, a higher antigen dose (5 microg ID93 vs. 2 microg) was associated with a greater incidence of adverse events (63.9% vs. 40.0%). H56:IC31 elicited strong T cell responses but was associated with transient cardiovascular events in 36% of vaccinees. Similarly, injection site reactions were more frequent in participants receiving the CAF01-adjuvanted H1 vaccine than in those given H1 alone. These findings illustrate that boosting immunity with adjuvants, particularly in LTBI - the primary target population for post-exposure vaccines, can involve safety trade-offs. Nonetheless, adjuvanted TB vaccines may still be less reactogenic than BCG revaccination, which has been associated with comparatively more adverse effects than two doses of H4:IC31 and H56:IC31.
Evaluation of Novel TB vaccines in clinical trials and regulatory barriers to implementation

Beyond biological and immunological challenges, demonstrating the safety and efficacy of multi-stage and post-exposure vaccines incorporating Mtb late-stage antigens is a demanding process. According to the FDA's vaccine development framework, phase I trials typically enrol 20-100 healthy Mtb-uninfected adults to assess escalating doses, safety, tolerability, and preliminary immunogenicity. Phase I trials may also enrol LTBI. While there is no requirement for participants to be BCG-vaccinated, if the trial is conducted in a country with a national BCG vaccination programme, all participants will likely have received BCG. Some of these trials include extended follow-up periods, such as 150 weeks for CAF01.

Phase II trials typically include hundreds of participants:including adults, adolescents, or LTBI:in randomized-controlled studies to refine dose and schedule, confirm safety, and evaluate immune responses. Phase II and IIb trials may also assess vaccine efficacy through prevention of conversion, prevention of infection or prevention of disease endpoints. In prevention of conversion and prevention of infection studies, IGRA/QFT-negative individuals are randomized to receive vaccine or placebo and monitored for IGRA/QFT conversion or sustained conversion as a surrogate of Mtb infection. In prevention of disease studies, LTBI (IGRA/QFT-positive) individuals are randomized and followed for progression to bacteriologically confirmed active pulmonary TB.

Phase III trials are large-scale, typically involving thousands of participants across multiple high-burden countries, and are double-blinded, randomised, and placebo-controlled. They assess protection against bacteriologically confirmed TB by comparing incidence rates between vaccine and placebo groups, while also identifying less common adverse events. A current phase III trial of M72/AS01_E recruits adolescents and adults, including HIV-positive individuals, in Indonesia, Kenya, Malawi, South Africa, and Zambia (NCT06062238). These trials require extended follow-ups (up to 49 months in NCT06062238), and must meet stringent efficacy benchmarks, with WHO recommending at least ~50% prevention of pulmonary TB in adults before a vaccine can be licensed (Fig. 3).

Regulatory requirements also pose major barriers to vaccine implementation. Under the FDA's vaccine development framework, manufacturers must demonstrate and secure approval for production processes, facilities, product characterization, and lot-to-lot consistency. Even when a vaccine is proven safe, effective, and licenced, post-exposure vaccination means targeting the vast population of nearly one-quarter of the global population with latent TB. The feasibility and affordability of rolling out such vaccines, therefore, need careful consideration, particularly in TB-endemic regions with limited resources and budgets.

Together, while new TB vaccines can, in principle, incorporate late-stage antigens, their stability issues, formulation complexity, increased reactogenicity, the demanding clinical approvals, and the multifaceted regulatory and implementation pathways make multi-stage and post-exposure TB vaccines difficult to realize in practice. Addressing these challenges will require diversifying the TB vaccine discovery pipeline, accelerating clinical development, and demonstrating public health impact through epidemiological studies. Funding, open science, and stakeholder engagement should be further strengthened to expedite vaccine development, approval, and distribution.
Examples of TB vaccines incorporating Mtb late-stage antigens, and the success story of M72/AS01_E as a post-exposure vaccine (Table 3)

Multi-stage subunit candidates, such as H56:IC31 and ID93 + GLA-SE, combine classical secreted proteins with latency-associated antigens. H56:IC31 consists of a recombinant fusion of Ag85B, ESAT-6, and the latency antigen Rv2660c, formulated with the IC31  adjuvant. ID93 + GLA-SE comprises a recombinant fusion of four Mtb antigens - the EsX family of virulence factors (Rv3619, Rv3620), the PE/PPE (Rv2608), and the latency antigen (Rv1813) - combined with the GLA-SE adjuvant. Both vaccines have demonstrated promising results in animal models and phase I clinical trials, with ID93 + GLA-SE also showing encouraging results in a phase II trial. However, it remains unclear whether either candidate can reliably prevent reactivation of latent infection and progression to active TB.

Thrice-administered H56:IC31 vaccination induced higher and faster-peaking frequencies of H56-specific IFN-gamma+TNF-alpha+IL-2+, IFN-gamma+TNF-alpha+, and IFN-gamma+ CD4+ T cells, as well as increased ESAT-6-specific cytokine+ CD4+ T cell responses in LTBI compared with uninfected vaccinees. However, Rv2660c showed poor immunogenicity in both QFT-negative and QFT-positive participants. Also, ESAT-6- and Rv2660c-specific CD4+ T cell responses were not consistently maintained through Day 292. A recently completed phase IIb trial in South Africa and Tanzania recruited HIV-negative adults who had successfully completed treatment for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB to evaluate whether H56:IC31 vaccination could reduce recurrence. Unexpectedly, the vaccine showed negative efficacy, with a 73.8% higher risk of recurrence compared to placebo. The majority of recurrences were due to relapse with the same strain. This underscores the importance of safety considerations for post-exposure vaccines and the need for synergistic, or at a minimum non-antagonistic, interactions between pre-existing and vaccine-induced immune responses to prevent severe Koch-like reactions, as discussed earlier.

Three doses of ID93 + GLA-SE in BCG-naive, healthy, QFT-negative participants preferentially induced IgG1 and IgG3 subclasses compared with ID93 alone, with these responses maintained for at least 6 months after the final dose. These antibodies mediated NK cell degranulation/activation in an antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity assay, as well as THP1 monocyte-driven antibody-dependent phagocytosis. Studied by day 70, the majority of vaccine-specific CD4+ T cells recognized Rv2608, with minimal responses detected against the other three antigens. This pattern is reminiscent of antigenic interference described earlier. ID93-specific CD4+ T cells produced various combinations of IL-2, TNF, and the activation marker CD154. In a phase I trial in healthy, BCG-vaccinated South Africans (both QFT-negative and QFT-positive), vaccination induced antigen-specific IgG and Th1 responses that peaked after two administrations. Notably, LTBI exhibited earlier boosting and stronger T cell responses compared with uninfected vaccinees. In a phase II trial in healthy, BCG-vaccinated, QFT-negative South Koreans, vaccination (versus placebo) elicited higher antigen-specific IgG levels, IFN-gamma-producing T cells, and IL-2+TNF+CD154+IFN-gamma+/- CD4+ T cell responses. These responses peaked after the first dose and were sustained for 12 months following the third vaccination. Overall, ID93 + GLA-SE demonstrated minimal capacity to induce CD8+ T cell responses across studies. A trial is currently recruiting both BCG-naive and BCG-vaccinated volunteers to evaluate the efficacy of ID93 + GLA-SE within an aerosol BCG-controlled human infection model (NCT06670755).

passages.text: Although it does not include late-stage antigens, the subunit vaccine M72/AS01_E has shown promise as a post-exposure TB vaccine. In a Phase IIb trial of 3575 adults in Kenya, South Africa, and Zambia, it demonstrated 49.7% efficacy over 3 years in preventing active TB among LTBI. M72 is a recombinant fusion protein comprising two early-stage Mtb antigens: Mtb32A (Rv0125), a probable serine protease, and Mtb39A (Rv1196, PPE18), a member of the PPE family. The AS01E adjuvant combines MPL and QS-21 in liposomes, with the "E" denoting a reduced dose suitable for paediatric use. M72/AS01_E elicited a high frequency of M72-specific CD4+ T cells producing various combinations of IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha, and IL-2, with minimal IL-17 expression. It also activated NK cells to produce antigen-specific IFN-gamma, and stimulated CD8+ T cell and IgG responses. CD4+ T cell and NK cell responses were stronger in LTBI than in those uninfected with Mtb, suggesting that the vaccine may act as a booster following natural infection. Furthermore, M72-specific IgG levels and CD4+ T cell frequencies increased after the first dose and remained elevated over the three-year follow-up period. Further studies are warranted to determine whether these immune features underlie the observed efficacy.
Concluding remark

As new TB vaccines progress through discovery stages toward clinical evaluations, an underlying challenge becomes increasingly apparent: the vast reservoir of individuals harbouring latent TB infection worldwide. This represents a major barrier to achieving global TB control and underscores the potential importance of including late-stage Mtb antigens in next-generation TB vaccines. These antigens, preferentially expressed during the latent, resuscitation, and reactivation phases of TB infection, hold promise for incorporation into multi-stage and post-exposure TB vaccines. Select candidate antigens should be HLA-promiscuous. At the same time, the development of post-exposure vaccines raises pertinent safety considerations, given the potential risk of reactivating the infection in latently infected individuals or triggering recurrence in cured patients.

This review compiled 10 latency-associated and four resuscitation-associated Mtb antigens that have demonstrated strong antigenicity in PBMCs and whole blood cultures from H-LTBI, and to a lesser extent, from active TB patients. These antigens also exhibited robust immunogenicity and protective efficacy in animal models and challenge studies. In silico analyses were subsequently performed to prioritize these candidates, and the shortlisted antigens were aligned with existing studies (Fig. 3). Finally, the challenges of incorporating late-stage antigens into multi-stage and post-exposure TB vaccines were discussed, alongside examples of post-exposure vaccine candidates currently undergoing clinical evaluation.

Collectively, this review highlights the significant contribution of late-stage Mtb antigens to immune responses against TB and their potential value in future vaccine design. Nevertheless, immunity to Mtb is complex, and validated correlates of protection remain elusive. Consequently, strong antigen-specific immune responses do not necessarily translate into protective efficacy, and protective immune responses observed in animal models may not fully reflect responses in humans. Ultimately, well-designed clinical trials remain definitive for determining the relevance, safety, and efficacy of novel TB vaccines incorporating late-stage antigens. Including LTBI - the main target group for post-exposure vaccines - in these trials is essential.

passages.text: Anticoagulants beyond coagulation: a narrative review of cardiovascular effects
Abstract

Anticoagulants are widely used to prevent and treat thrombotic disorders, and continuous advances have refined their efficacy and safety. Beyond their established anticoagulant function, growing evidence indicates that some agents exert additional cardiovascular effects through pleiotropic mechanisms. In this narrative review, we examine both the intended and potential unintended effects of anticoagulants, with particular attention to their actions beyond coagulation. We discuss their influence on vascular pathology and cardiac function, highlighting distinctions between different anticoagulant classes. A deeper understanding of these pleiotropic effects may help guide future research, improve long-term outcomes, and support more targeted therapeutic strategies for patients most likely to benefit.
Introduction

Anticoagulants inhibit the coagulation cascade to prevent or treat thrombosis. Historically, two main classes emerged in the early 20th century. The first comprised unfractionated heparin (UFH), glycosaminoglycans of variable chain length purified from animal tissue, which accelerate antithrombin (AT)-dependent inactivation of serine proteases, including FXa and thrombin. The next generation included low molecular weight heparins (LMWHs), less heterogeneous and enriched in AT-binding capacity, and the synthetic pentasaccharide fondaparinux.

The second class of oral anticoagulants (OACs) consisted of vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), based on the discovery that coumarins:derived from dicoumarol in spoiled sweet clover:inhibit vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of coagulation proteins. Over half a century later, direct OACs (DOACs) were developed as small molecules targeting FXa or thrombin. More recently, FXIa inhibitors have emerged as a novel class with potential safety advantages. In addition, RNA silencing therapies and monoclonal antibodies, mostly targeting FXI(a), are in (pre)clinical testing.

While anticoagulants aim to prevent thrombosis, their principal unintended effect is bleeding. Both efficacy (thrombus inhibition) and safety (bleeding risk) depend on anticoagulation intensity. Beyond fibrin inhibition, anticoagulants can also modulate fibrinolysis, platelets, and endothelial function, contributing to both antithrombotic and bleeding-prone actions, as well as pleiotropic effects, including anti-inflammatory properties. This review examines the intended and unintended cardiovascular effects of current anticoagulants.
Pharmacological properties of anticoagulants
Parenteral anticoagulants: LMWHs and direct thrombin inhibitors

UFH and LMWH act by amplifying the rate of coagulation protease inactivation by the natural serine protease inhibitor AT. Binding of UFH to AT results in a conformational change in the latter, thereby rendering it a rapid and irreversible inhibitor of FXa and thrombin, and probably also of FIXa, FXIa, and FXIIa. Subsequently, heparin dissociates from the complex for reuse. This mechanism is responsible for the largest anticoagulant effect. The molecular weight of heparin is variable, and only one-third of UFH molecules possess the unique AT-binding site.

Two additional mechanisms of action have been described. Firstly, at higher concentrations (>=5 units/mL) and in the presence of heparin cofactor II, heparin can catalyse thrombin inhibition without the AT-binding site. Secondly, at very high concentrations, heparin inhibits FXa activation by binding FIXa, independently of AT and heparin cofactor II.

Heparin is administered parenterally as it is not absorbed from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Bioavailability with subcutaneous administration is lower compared with intravenous administration (Table 1). Owing to its strong negative charge, UFH molecules associate with the vascular endothelium, releasing proteins, such as lipoprotein lipase that are physiologically attached to endothelial glycosaminoglycans, including heparan sulfate.

Heparin clearance is biphasic: rapid cellular uptake by endothelial cells and macrophages, followed by slower renal elimination. Clearance is dose-dependent, leading to a variable half-life. In addition, the anticoagulant response varies between patients. Therefore, the anticoagulant effect should be monitored using the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) or an anti-Xa assay. In cases where heparin doses are higher (e.g. in cardiopulmonary bypass surgeries), the activated clotting time is used. The anticoagulant effect of heparin is rapidly reversed by administration of protamine.

Depolymerizing UFH to about one-third of its molecular weight produces LMWH. Smaller LMWH fragments (<18 saccharide units) cannot bind both AT and thrombin simultaneously; thus, LMWH primarily targets FXa.

Compared with UFH, LMWH binds less to plasma proteins and cells, resulting in more predictable pharmacology, a longer half-life, and stable anticoagulant effects (Table 1). Its predictable dose-response allows weight-adjusted dosing in most patients, and reduced endothelial binding enhances subcutaneous bioavailability.

LMWHs are mainly cleared renally; impaired renal function prolongs half-life, sometimes requiring dose adjustment based on peak anti-Xa levels. Their anticoagulant effect is only partially reversed by protamine.

UFH is primarily used in emergent vascular interventions or cardiopulmonary bypass, while LMWH is common for prophylaxis and treatment of venous thromboembolism (VTE), and in patients for whom OACs are contraindicated, such as during pregnancy or in cancer (Table 2).

passages.text: Fondaparinux is a synthetic pentasaccharide containing only the AT-binding site, selectively enhancing FXa inhibition. With a half-life of ~17 h, once-daily subcutaneous dosing achieves therapeutic levels. Its clearance is almost entirely renal, so it is contraindicated in severe renal insufficiency. Monitoring can be done with anti-FXa assays. Although no specific antidote exists, recombinant FVIIa may partially reverse its effect.

Unlike UFH, LMWH, and fondaparinux, direct thrombin inhibitors (DTIs) inhibit thrombin independently of AT. Approved parenteral DTIs include bivalirudin and argatroban. Hirudin, the natural prototype, inspired the shorter synthetic analogue bivalirudin. Bivalent DTIs (hirudin, bivalirudin) bind thrombin at both its active site and exosite 1, while univalent DTIs (argatroban) bind only the active site. DTIs inhibit both soluble and fibrin-bound thrombin.

Bivalirudin is metabolized by proteolysis and hepatic metabolism, though renal impairment may prolong its half-life. Argatroban is primarily metabolized by the liver, requiring dose adjustment in hepatic dysfunction. The anticoagulant effect of DTIs is monitored by aPTT, particularly in patients at high bleeding risk, as no specific antidote is available.
Vitamin K antagonists

Vitamin K is a coenzyme essential for synthesizing vitamin K-dependent coagulation proteins (FII, FVII, FIX, FX, protein C, S, and Z) and several other hepatic and extrahepatic proteins. It undergoes continuous recycling via reduction and oxidation, mediated by the vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1 (VKORC1). VKAs inhibit VKORC1, inducing functional vitamin K deficiency in hepatocytes and depleting active coagulation factors. Consequently, their anticoagulant effect can be reversed by administering vitamin K. VKAs also affect extrahepatic vitamin K-dependent proteins:17 are known:including osteocalcin, matrix Gla protein (MGP), and growth arrest-specific 6 (Gas6).

passages.text: VKAs are administered orally. Due to the long half-lives of FII and FX, several days of concurrent heparin are required to reach the narrow therapeutic window. Management of VKAs is challenging due to individual variability and interactions with medications and diet, requiring dose adjustments based on the international normalized ratio (INR), a standardized measure of prothrombin time (PT). Fiix-assay studies:suggesting that FII and FX predominantly determine thrombin generation under VKA treatment and that FVII exhibits marked variability:indicate that measuring FII and FX instead of the INR may provide more stable anticoagulation, but this assay is not yet routinely applied.

VKAs are rapidly absorbed in the stomach and small intestine, with almost complete oral bioavailability. Plasma protein binding is high, resulting in a low free plasma concentration that is pharmacologically active. Acenocoumarol has the shortest half-life, followed by warfarin and phenprocoumon (Table 3). The long half-life of phenprocoumon is attributed to slower CYP-mediated clearance, as well as enterohepatic recycling.
