passages.text: Multi-index quality evaluation of licorice from six Chinese origins using entropy factor analysis and systematic clustering

This study aimed to establish a comprehensive evaluation system for assessing the quality and classification of licorice from six different origins in China using multiple indicators, including combustion heat, combustion stability, fat, crude fiber, ash, trace element, glycyrrhizic acid (GLA), liquiritin (LI), and amino acid contents. Six types of licorice from Dongsheng District in Ordos, Inner Mongolia, Huimin District in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, Guyang County in Baotou, Inner Mongolia, Linhe District in Bayanzhuoer City, Xinjiang, Kashgar Prefecture in Xinjiang, and Yining County in Yili, Xinjiang, were selected as research objects to determine the combustion heat, combustion stability, fat, crude fiber, ash, trace element, glycyrrhizic acid (GLA), liquiritin (LI), and amino acid contents. The heat of combustion is a crucial metric for assessing the energy content of substances, thereby reflecting the quality of medicinal materials. The thermal stability of traditional Chinese herbal medicines is associated primarily with their ability to preserve their chemical structure and biological activity when subjected to heating processes, such as boiling, brewing, heating, or storage. Using gray pattern recognition (GPR), entropy factor analysis (EFA), and systematic clustering analysis (SCA), comprehensive evaluation systems were constructed for six licorice samples based on nutritional indicators, including multiple indicators of the heat of combustion, combustibility (licorice combustion stability), fat content, amino acid content, ash content, crude fiber content, glycyrrhizic acid (GLA), liquiritin (LI), and trace element content. Using entropy factor analysis based on 39 variables, the quality ranking of the six licorice samples was as follows: licorice from Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia > licorice from Yining County, Yili, Xinjiang> licorice from Guyang County, Baotou, Inner Mongolia> licorice from Hohhot Huimin District, Inner Mongolia> licorice from Kashgar Prefecture, Xinjiang > licorice from Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer City, Inner Mongolia. The results of the systematic clustering analysis (SCA) indicated that the licorice samples could be classified into three distinct categories and that the 39 variables could be grouped into four groups. This study has significant theoretical and practical implications for the determination and comprehensive evaluation of multiple quality indicators of licorice.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12870-026-08467-0.
Introduction

Licorice (Glycyrrhiza uralensis Fisch), a traditional Chinese medicinal herb, has been used in Chinese medicine for thousands of years. It has a wide range of pharmacological effects, including anti-inflammatory, antiviral, antioxidant, and hepatoprotective properties. In recent years, licorice has been increasingly studied, and its applications in food and cosmetics have attracted attention. However, the quality and efficacy of licorice are closely related to its chemical composition, and there are significant differences in the components of licorice samples from different sources, which directly affects their effectiveness. Therefore, establishing a scientific and objective comprehensive evaluation system to assess the quality of licorice samples is essential.

Nutritional indicators are core components. The combustion heat is an important index for measuring the energy content of a substance and reflects the total amount of combustible materials in licorice. The combustibility, particularly the combustion stability, of licorice is directly related to its safety and effectiveness during processing and use.Fat content is an important parameter for evaluating the nutritional value of licorice, as it affects its pharmacological activity and stability. Trace elements and amino acids present in Chinese herbal medicines constitute two fundamental chemical components that establish a connection between their material basis and pharmacological effects, indicating the quality of the medicinal materials. The crude fiber content represents the quantity of indigestible plant material, which affects the digestibility and potential therapeutic effectiveness of the herb. The ash content denotes the total mineral content, offering insights into the presence of essential inorganic compounds and the potential for contamination.

Owing to differences in their planting environments, cultivation methods, and harvesting processes, licorice from different regions exhibit significant quality variations. These differences impact not only the medicinal efficacy of licorice but also its market value. Therefore, studying the quality differences of licorice from various regions and systematically evaluating them through multi-index quantitative analysis methods is essential for the standardized cultivation and quality control of licorice.Traditionally, research on licorice quality has focused on the analysis of single indicators, such as active components (e.g., glycyrrhizic acid and liquiritin).

In summary, no detailed reports have focused on constructing a quality evaluation system for licorice based on the heat of combustion, combustion stability, fat, crude fiber, ash, trace element, glycyrrhizic acid (GLA), liquiritin (LI), and amino acid contents of licorice. To address this gap, we can refer to methods used for evaluating other plants and adapt them to the unique characteristics of licorice for a comprehensive assessment.This study builds on indicators such as combustion heat, combustion stability, fat content, crude fiber content, ash content, trace element content, glycyrrhizic acid (GLA), liquiritin (LI), and amino acid content to explore the quality differences of licorice from different production areas and establish an evaluation system. This approach precisely addresses the shortcomings of previous studies on licorice quality. Currently, there is extensive research on licorice, both domestically and internationally.

The study selected six types of licorice from various regions as research objects, including Dongsheng District of Ordos in Inner Mongolia, Huimin District of Hohhot in Inner Mongolia, Guyang County in Baotou in Inner Mongolia, Linhe District of Bayanzhuoer City in Xinjiang, Kashgar District in Xinjiang, and Yining County, Yili in Xinjiang. This study assessed parameters such as the heat of combustion, combustion stability, fat content, crude fiber, ash, trace elements, glycyrrhizic acid (GLA), liquiritin (LI), and amino acids in licorice from six different origins. This study established a multi-index analysis and evaluation system for licorice from different sources, providing a reference for quality control and the development and utilization of licorice byproducts.
Materials and methods
Materials and instruments
Test material

Six types of licorice (cultivated), the dried roots of the leguminous plant Glycyrrhiza uralensis Fisch, Licorice samples from Dongsheng District of Ordos Inner Mongolia (Figure S4), Huimin District of Hohhot of Inner Mongolia (Figure S5), Guyang County of Baotou of Inner Mongolia (Figure S6), Linhe District of Bayanzhuoer City (Figure S7), Xinjiang Kashgar Prefecture (Figure S8), and Yili Yining County of Xinjiang (Figure S9) were used as analysis samples and were purchased from Laibin Chinese herbal medicine market in Guangxi, China. The corresponding Figures S4-S9 are available in the Supplementary Materials. Licorice samples of six different origins were dried, ground using a mortar, and screened through 40 mesh pharmacopoeias. Identification was conducted by Prof. Caiyun Jiang of Guangxi Science & Technology Normal University, and the samples were stored at Guangxi Science & Technology Normal University.

Licorice originated from Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia, production date: January 2021; licorice originated from Hohhot Huimin District, Inner Mongolia, production date: January 2021; licorice originated from Guyang County, Baotou, Inner Mongolia, production date: November 2020; licorice originated from Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer City, Xinjiang, production date: December 2020; licorice originated from Kashgar Prefecture, Xinjiang, production date: November 2020; licorice originated from Yining County, Yili, Xinjiang, production date: October 2020.
Instrument

The combustion heat determination included an HR-15 oxygen bomb calorimeter, ignition wire (nickel-chromium wire), tablet press (Hunan Changsha Changxing Higher Education Instrument and Equipment Development Co., Ltd.), pulverizer (FW135 type, Tianjin Tester Instrument Co., Ltd.), crucible, STA2500 synchronous thermal analyzer (NETZSCH, Germany), F1600 automatic fiber tester (Jinan Alva Instrument Co., Ltd.), GZX-GF101-3-S drying oven (Shanghai Huyueming Scientific Instrument Co., Ltd.), SE206 fat analyzer (Jinan Alva Instrument Co., Ltd.), SX-4-10P muffle furnace (Tianjin Teste Instrument Co., Ltd.), FA2004 electronic analytical balance (Shanghai Sunny Hengping Scientific Instrument Co., Ltd.), ICP-OES spectrometer (iCAP 7000 SERIES, Thermo Scientific, USA), 300 amino acid analyzer (German Mann Bohr), LC-2050 high-performance liquid chromatograph (Shimadzu Corporation, Japan), circulating water vacuum pump (Shanghai Lingde Instrument Co., Ltd.), 2 ml sample vial, and disposable needle filter (mixed fiber-aqueous system) (Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.).
Reagent

Benzoic acid (analytical pure, Tianjin Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.); petroleum ether (boiling range of 30 ~ 60 C, Chengdu Jinshan Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.); 2,006,003 pharmaceutical capsules (Guangdong Biotech Co., Ltd.); potassium hydroxide (Tianjin Damao Technology Co., Ltd.), hydrochloric acid (Xilong Science Co., Ltd.), sulfuric acid (Xilong Science Co., Ltd.), multielement mixed liquid standard samples (GNM-M218741-2013), 30% hydrogen peroxide (Xilong Science Co., Ltd.), nitric acid (Chengdu Jinshan Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.), amino acid mixed standards 650 - 0037 Feedstuff (German Mannmabol Co., Ltd.), ninhydrin hydrate (Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.), methanol (Guangzhou Tongyuan Chemical Technology Co., Ltd.), phosphoric acid (Tianjin Damao Chemical Reagent Factory), liquiritin (Shanghai Yuanye Biotechnology Co., Ltd.), glycyrrhizic acid (Shanghai Yuanye Biotechnology Co., Ltd.), and acetonitrile (Guangzhou Tongyuan Chemical Technology Co., Ltd.) were used.
Related experimental methods

The ash content, trace element content, heat of combustion, fat content, thermogravimetric parameters, and crude fiber content of the six types of licorice were determined according to previously described methods.

Thermogravimetric analysis conditions: The experimental procedure involved increasing the test temperature from 25 C to 600 C at a rate of 20 K/min under a high-purity nitrogen gas atmosphere. The specific conditions for the analysis were as follows: a heating rate of 2.5 C/min and the use of high-purity nitrogen gas as the atmosphere. An empty crucible was used as the reference material.

Methods for determining amino acids involve the use of wavelengths of 570 nm and 440 nm. The procedure requires the addition of ascorbic acid, which serves as a coreagent activator, to the ninhydrin solution, which acts as a reagent for the derivator. This mixture was thoroughly shaken and stored in the dark for a minimum of four hours. The mixture was subsequently transferred to a reagent bottle, resulting in a color change from yellow to purple. The recommended ratio is 40 mg of activator to 100 ml of ninhydrin. A 0.4 g sample (accurate to four decimal places) was accurately weighed in a dry 50 mL volumetric flask, and a diluted hydrochloric acid solution (1 mL of hydrochloric acid was measured, and ultrapure water was added to a 1000 mL volumetric flask) was used for 0.5 h, after which the diluted hydrochloric acid was used to dissolve the sample in a 50 mL volumetric flask for backup.

At wavelengths of 570 and 440 nm, the 20 amino acids were optimally separated under the given conditions. Amino acid profiles were automatically generated, and the amino acid content was calculated by processing peak areas. The peak spectrum of the amino acid content of licorice in Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia is shown in Fig. 1. A comprehensive evaluation system was developed to analyze multiple indicators of licorice from six different origins, including combustion heat, combustion stability, fat content, ash content, crude fiber, trace elements, and amino acids.
Peak spectrum of the amino acid content of licorice in Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia

Determination of glycyrrhizic acid (GLA) and liquiritin (LI) contents: A 2 g sample was accurately weighed onto filter paper and dried at 60 C for 12 h. The dried sample (0.1 g) was accurately weighed into a 25 mL volumetric flask, and a 67% methanol aqueous solution was added. The mixture was soaked at room temperature for 24 h, sonicated for 30 min, allowed to return to room temperature, diluted to the mark with a 67% methanol aqueous solution, filtered through a 0.22 mum membrane, and analyzed according to the HPLC operating procedures. The GLA and LI HPLC chromatograms of licorice in Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia, are shown in Figures S10-S11 (Supplementary Materials).
The test was repeated three times for each sample (n = 3, RSD%<2%).
Results and discussion
Licorice thermogravimetric analysis
Licorice in Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia.

Figure 2a and Table S1(a) show that licorice lost weight at 36.3 C, with a loss of 3.34%. When the temperature reached 146.5 C, licorice entered the second weight-loss stage, and when the temperature rose to 394.3 C, the loss rate of licorice reached 42.29%. The licorice decomposed further, resulting in weight loss and a residual mass of 42.17%. The DTG curve of Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia, licorice exhibited two peak morphologies with inflection points at 119.5  C and 310.2  C. The DTA curve showed two exothermic peaks in the temperature range of 41.0-151.2 C, with peak areas of 154.6 J/g and 14.56 J/g and peak temperatures of 114.7 C and 375.4 C, respectively.

a Thermal analysis of licorice in Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia b Thermal analysis of licorice in the Hohhot Huimin area, Inner Mongolia c Thermal analysis of licorice in Guyang County, Baotou, Inner Mongolia d Thermal analysis of licorice in Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer city, Xinjiang e Thermal analysis of licorice in Kashgar Prefecture, Xinjiang f Thermal analysis of licorice in Yining County, Yili, Xinjiang
Licorice in Hohhot Huimin District, Inner Mongolia.

Figure 2b and Table S1(b) show that licorice began losing weight at 40.7 C, and the loss rate was 4.10% at this temperature. At 182.3 C, licorice entered the second weight loss stage, and the loss rate of licorice was 52.23%. When the temperature reached 429.7 C, it entered the third weight loss stage. At 599.1 C, the loss rate of licorice was 7.28%. Ultimately, licorice continued to decompose, resulting in a remaining mass as low as 34.91%. The DTG curve of licorice from the Hohhot Huimin area in Inner Mongolia showed a single peak with an inflection point at 312.7  C. The DTA curve exhibited a significant exothermic peak at 117.1 C, with a peak area of 129.5 J/g and a temperature range of 44.4-155.0 C.
Licorice in Guyang County, Baotou, Inner Mongolia.

As shown in Fig. 2c and Table S1 (c), licorice began to lose weight at 41.3 C, and the loss rate of licorice was 3.02% at this temperature. When the temperature reached 147.6 C, licorice entered the second weightlessness stage, and when the temperature rose to 407.4 C, the loss rate of licorice reached 50.49%. Licorice was further decomposed weightlessly, and its residual mass was 35.01%.

The DTG curve of licorice in Guyang County, Baotou, Inner Mongolia, showed two peaks, with inflection points at 108.5 and 308.7  C. The DTA curve showed a significant exothermic peak at 110.6 C, with a peak area of 91.57 J/g and a temperature range of 40.8-146.7 C.
Licorice in Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer city, Xinjiang.

As illustrated in Fig. 2d and Table S1(d), the weight loss in licorice commenced at 49.3 C, with a loss rate of 6.10%. Upon reaching 153.8 C, the second stage of weight loss commenced, and upon reaching 397.6 C, the loss rate of licorice reached 50.31%. As the temperature continued to increase, the licorice became increasingly weightless and decomposed, resulting in a final mass of 27.28%.

The DTG curve exhibited two distinct peak shapes, with inflection points at 85.6  C and 305.0  C. The DTA curve of licorice in Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer City, Xinjiang, exhibited a pronounced exothermic peak, with a peak value of 113.5 C, a temperature range of 34.7-166.5 C, and a peak area of 260.7 J/g.
Licorice in Kashgar Prefecture, Xinjiang.

As shown in Fig. 2e and Table S1(e), licorice in the Kashgar region of Xinjiang reached the weight-loss stage at 45.4 C, corresponding to a loss rate of 3.22%. At 150.7 C, the licorice entered the second weight-loss stage. Upon further increasing the temperature to 397.6 C, the rate of licorice loss was 49.57%. The licorice was then subjected to further weight loss, resulting in a residual mass of 34.18%.

The DTG curve of licorice in Kashgar Prefecture, Xinjiang, exhibited two peaks, with inflection points at 108.9 and 309.6  C. The DTA curve demonstrated a pronounced exothermic peak at 117.9 C, with a peak area of 167.5 J/g and a temperature range of 36.4-158.2 C.
Licorice in Yining County, Yili, Xinjiang.

As shown in Fig. 2f and Table S1(f), weight loss in licorice commenced at 44.8 C in Yili Yining County, Xinjiang, and the loss rate of licorice was 8.61% at this temperature. Upon reaching 162.6 C, licorice commenced the second weight-loss stage, with a loss rate of 8.61% at this temperature. At 390.6 C, the loss rate reached 50.16%. As the temperature continued to increase, licorice entered the third weight-loss stage, with a loss rate of 19.25% at 598.7  C. The final quality of licorice was 21.50%.

The DTG curve of licorice in Yining County, Yili, Xinjiang, exhibited two peaks, with inflection points at 95.5 and 312.7  C. The DTA curve exhibited a pronounced exothermic peak at 108.9 C, spanning a temperature range of 34.4-177.7 C, and peaked area of 287.70 J/g. Additionally, an endothermic peak was observed at 295.9  C, with a peak area of 96.00 J/g and a temperature range of 251.5-367.4  C.

When the temperature reached a maximum of 182.3 C, the first stage of water loss ended, with the water loss rate for licorice ranging from 3.2% to 8.7%. Within the temperature range of 305.0 to 312.7 C, licorice began to decompose proteins, crude fats, carbohydrates, and other substances. In the third stage, the crude fiber components of licorice decompose. The higher the heating rate is, the more pronounced the temperature lag phenomenon, yielding higher measured values for both the initial and final temperatures of weight loss and a broader decomposition temperature range.

The combustion stability of licorice from six different origins was analyzed using combustion parameter data. The licorice samples were sourced from the following locations: Dongsheng District of Ordos, Inner Mongolia; Huhhot Huimin District, Inner Mongolia; Guyang County, Baotou, Inner Mongolia; Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer City, Inner Mongolia; Kashgar Prefecture, Xinjiang; and Yining County, Yili, Xinjiang. Thermogravimetry was employed to study the combustion characteristics of licorice at various heating rates using a thermogravimetric analyzer, which helped in determining the combustion stability. This study utilized the gray pattern recognition method, and EXCEL was used to calculate the F values of the six licorice samples, which were 0.7127, 0.6933, 0.6621, 0.7225, 0.6777, and 0.8770. The combustion stability ranking of the six licorice samples was as follows: licorice from Yining County, Xinjiang > licorice from Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer City, Inner Mongolia > licorice from Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia > licorice from Hohhot Huimin District, Inner Mongolia > licorice from Kashgar Prefecture, Xinjiang > licorice from Guyang County, Baotou, Inner Mongolia. The ranking of combustion stability serves as a guide for processing and storage decisions, identifying licorice from Yining County, Xinjiang as possessing superior thermal stability. Variations in combustion stability can be attributed to diverse chemical compositions influenced by the geographic and climatic conditions of each region. These findings offer valuable insights for selecting licorice sources based on their thermal stability for industrial use.

The optimal wavelengths, correlation coefficients (R), and instrument detection limits for the elements are listed in Table S2 (supplementary materials). Only licorice in Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia, contained 0.0883 microg/g Co. The Pb content ranged from 1.84 to 6.01 microg/g, with an average value of 4.0567 microg/g. All 6 types of licorice contained seven essential amino acids (Trp was not detected), namely, Thr, Val, Met, Ile, Leu, Phe and Lys. The ratio of the content of essential amino acids to the total content of amino acids in the human body ranged from 6.34% to 26.58%, and the ratio of the content of essential amino acids to the content of non-essential amino acids in the human body ranged from 6.77% to 36.21%.

There are differences in the amino acid content of licorice in different production areas, which may be related to the climate, planting environment, and processing methods of each licorice production area.
Development of a multi-indicator system for evaluating licorice quality
Entropy factor analysis

Entropy factor analysis (EFA) integrates information entropy and factor analysis to reduce multivariate data and extract relevant features. The entropy coefficients of the samples were used to replace the sample correlation coefficient matrix in factor analysis, the entropy correlation coefficients were used to participate in the computation and obtain the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and the variance contribution ratio and total variance contribution ratio of the entropy factor analysis were computed. Given the extensive number of indicators (39) incorporated in this study, entropy factor analysis was employed to reduce the dimensionality and identify the most informative factors.

After performing entropy factor analysis, the cumulative contribution (Table 1) of the first 5 entropy factors reached 100.00%>85%, so the first 5 entropy factors were selected, which represented 100.00% of the 39 variables, including the stability of combustion, QV, ash, crude fiber, fat, Al, Ba, Cr, Cu, Fe, K, Li, Mg, Mn, Na, Ni, Sr, Zn, CySO3H, Asp, MetSON, Thr, Ser, Glu, Gly, Ala, (Cys)2, Val, Met, Ile, Leu, Tyr, Phe, His, Lys, glycyrrhizic acid (GLA), liquiritin (LI), Arg and Pro, in six types of licorice from Dongsheng District in Ordos, Inner Mongolia, Huimin District in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, Guyang County in Baotou, Inner Mongolia, Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer City, Xinjiang, Kashgar Prefecture in Xinjiang, and Yining County in Yili, Xinjiang.

This ranking was determined from composite entropy factor scores, which were calculated via the weighted least squares approach, with weights representing the eigenroots of the entropy factors (F1-F5) and composite entropy factor scores (F), with weights representing the eigenroots of the entropy factors. The formula employed was F = 0.3075 F1 + 0.2230 F2+ 0.1901 F3+ 0.1747 F4+ 0.1047 F5.

The entropy factor scores and composite entropy factor scores (Table 3) of the 39 variables, including the stability of combustion, QV, ash, crude fiber, fat, Al, Ba, Cr, Cu, Fe, K, Li, Mg, Mn, Na, Ni, Sr, Zn, CySO3H, Asp, MetSON, Thr, Ser, Glu, Gly, Ala, (Cys)2, Val, Met, Ile, Leu, Tyr, Phe, His, Lys, glycyrrhizic acid (GLA), liquiritin (LI), Arg, and Pro, the entropy factor score order of the six licorice samples was as follows: licorice of Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia > licorice of Yining County, Yili, Xinjiang> licorice of Guyang County, Baotou, Inner Mongolia> licorice of Hohhot Huimin District, Inner Mongolia> licorice of Kashgar Prefecture, Xinjiang > licorice of Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer City, Inner Mongolia. The results of the multi-indicator evaluation of 39 variables revealed that the licorice of Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia, had the highest quality, followed by the licorice of Yining County, Yili, Xinjiang. The findings indicate substantial variations in the quality of licorice from different regions, with Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia being identified as the source of the highest quality. These insights can inform sourcing decisions for medicinal, nutritional, and industrial applications, thereby enhancing product efficacy and safety. All the samples were purchased from the same herbal medicine market rather than being collected directly from their places of origin. These findings suggest that the samples may be subject to postharvest influences, such as storage and transportation, which may affect their ability to accurately represent differences attributable solely to their origin.

Systematic clustering analysis (SCA)

Systematic clustering analysis (SCA) is a statistical method for grouping data based on similarities and correlations. The 39 variables, including the stability of combustion, QV, ash, crude fiber, fat, Al, Ba, Cr, Cu, Fe, K, Li, Mg, Mn, Na, Ni, Sr, Zn, CySO3H, Asp, MetSON, Thr, Ser, Glu, Gly, Ala, (Cys)2, Val, Met, Ile, Leu, Tyr, Phe, His, Lys, glycyrrhizic acid (GLA), liquiritin (LI), Arg and Pro, and six types of licorice from Dongsheng District in Ordos, Inner Mongolia, Huimin District in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, Guyang County in Baotou, Inner Mongolia, Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer City, Xinjiang, Kashgar Prefecture in Xinjiang, and Yining County in Yili, Xinjiang, can be classified into three categories (Fig. 3a). Licorice from Huimin District in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, Guyang County in Baotou, Inner Mongolia, and Kashgar Prefecture in Xinjiang were classified into one category. Licorice from Dongsheng District in Ordos, Inner Mongolia, was grouped into one category, and licorice from Yining County in Yili and Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer City, Xinjiang, was grouped into another category. This is consistent with the results of the entropy factor analysis.
a Systematic clustering analysis (SCA) of 6 licorice samples b Systematic clustering analysis (SCA) for 39 variables of 6 licorice samples

The 39 variables were classified into four groups (Fig. 3b). The variables Cu, Ni, Cr, Al, Val, Mg, Mn, (Cys)2, fat, Lys, Ba, Fe, Ile, Pro, and Met were clustered into one category. The analysis primarily conveys information regarding energy and trace elements, which are essential components of nutrition and play crucial roles in maintaining overall health and well-being. Crude fiber, Arg, combustion stability, QV, Li, Leu, Tyr, K, and Ser were clustered into one category, which reflected the quality of licorice from the perspective of combustion. CySO3H, Ala, Gly, MetSON, His, LI, and Zn were clustered into a category that broadly encompasses biochemistry and chemistry, with a particular focus on amino acids, chemical compounds, and elements involved in biological processes. These components, including ash, Na, Sr, Asp, Thr, Glu, GLA, and Phe, are clustered into one category, which is essential for various metabolic processes and overall physiological health. Minerals (ash, Na, and Sr) are inorganic elements that play crucial roles in maintaining physiological functions, such as fluid balance (Na), bone health (Sr), and overall mineral balance. Amino acids (Asp, Thr, Glu, and Phe) are protein building blocks involved in a wide range of biological processes.
Conclusion

Through entropy factor analysis, on the basis of 39 variables, including the stability of combustion, QV, ash, crude fiber, fat, Al, Ba, Cr, Cu, Fe, K, Li, Mg, Mn, Na, Ni, Sr, Zn, CySO3H, Asp, MetSON, Thr, Ser, Glu, Gly, Ala, (Cys)2, Val, Met, Ile, Leu, Tyr, Phe, His, Lys, glycyrrhizic acid (GLA), liquiritin (LI), Arg and Pro, the quality rankings of the six licorice samples were as follows: licorice of Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia > licorice of Yining County, Yili, Xinjiang> licorice of Guyang County, Baotou, Inner Mongolia> licorice of Hohhot Huimin District, Inner Mongolia> licorice of Kashgar Prefecture, Xinjiang > licorice of Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer City, Inner Mongolia. The multi-indicator evaluation of 39 variables revealed that Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia, produced the highest quality licorice.

The gray pattern recognition (GPR) method was used to assess the stability of licorice combustion. The results demonstrated that the combustion stability rankings of the six licorice samples were as follows: licorice of Yining County, Yili, Xinjiang > licorice of Linhe District, Bayanzhuoer city, Inner Mongolia > licorice of Dongsheng District, Ordos, Inner Mongolia > licorice of Hohhot Huimin District, Inner Mongolia > licorice of Kashgar Prefecture, Xinjiang > licorice of Guyang County, Baotou, Inner Mongolia.

Systematic clustering analysis (SCA) revealed that the licorice samples could be classified into three categories and that the 39 variables could be divided into four groups. In this study, we constructed a comprehensive evaluation system for six licorice samples based on nutritional indicators, including multiple indicators of heat of combustion, combustibility (licorice combustion stability), fat content, amino acid content, ash content, crude fiber content, glycyrrhizic acid (GLA) content, liquiritin (LI) content, and trace element content, using gray pattern recognition (GPR), entropy factor analysis (EFA), and systematic clustering analysis (SCA).This study has substantial theoretical and practical implications for the determination and comprehensive evaluation of multiple quality indicators of licorice, particularly in assessing its quality and classification.

passages.text: Protocol to reconstitute motor protein clustering on vesicle membranes using a DNA scaffold-based system in vitro
Summary

Cytoskeletal motor proteins drive long-range intracellular transport, but how their organization on vesicle membranes affects motility remains poorly understood. Here, we present a protocol to reconstitute kinesin-1 clustering on synthetic liposomes using a DNA-based scaffold. We describe steps for functionalizing liposomes with kinesin-1, inducing DNA-mediated motor clusters, and analyzing liposome motility on surface-immobilized microtubules. This protocol enables quantitative investigation of motor organization in vesicle transport and is adaptable to other cytoskeletal motors.
For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Jiang et al.
Graphical abstract
Highlights
Steps for assembling and isolating kinesin-functionalized liposomes
Procedures for inducing and verifying motor clustering on liposome surfaces
Guidance on quantifying motor number and comparing motility of clustered motors

Here, we present a protocol to reconstitute kinesin-1 clustering on synthetic liposomes using a DNA-based scaffold. We describe steps for functionalizing liposomes with kinesin-1, inducing DNA-mediated motor clusters, and analyzing liposome motility on surface-immobilized microtubules. This protocol enables quantitative investigation of motor organization in vesicle transport and is adaptable to other cytoskeletal motors.
Before you begin
Innovation

Teams of cytoskeletal motors drive long-range intracellular vesicle transport, yet how motor organization on vesicle membrane quantitatively modulates motility remains poorly understood. Although dynein clustering into lipid microdomains has been observed in vivo, and kinesin clustering on liposomes has been qualitatively explored through cholesterol/sphingomyelin-mediated phase separation, existing approaches lack the ability to precisely control motor organization and rigorously quantify its functional consequences.

This protocol advances the field by integrating established biochemical and biophysical techniques into a unified, quantitative workflow for studying motor clustering on synthetic vesicles. SNAP-tagged motor proteins are covalently conjugated to DNA oligos and anchored to liposomes, while a programmable, fluorescent DNA scaffold induces clustering of defined motor numbers. Rather than inferring motor copy number from mixing ratios, this workflow directly measures motor number on liposomes using fluorescence intensity analysis, enabling quantitative comparison of motility in unclustered versus clustered conditions.

Key innovations include (1) a DNA-based clustering scaffold that allows precise and tunable control over motor copy number within clusters, and (2) a rigorous analysis framework that maps experimentally measured motor number to vesicle motility, avoiding ambiguities arising from stochastic motor attachment. By combining DNA-protein conjugation, liposome flotation, single-particle fluorescence quantification, and motility assays into a single protocol, this method enables systemic interrogation of how motor organization shapes vesicle transport. The modular design further allows straightforward adaptation to other cytoskeletal motors, motor mutants, or clustering architectures.
Conjugation of BG-GLA-NHS to amino-modified DNA oligo
Timing: 4 h
Desalt into 200 mM sodium borate (pH 8.5) using a Sephadex G-25 desalting column.
Measure concentration using a Nanodrop.
Resuspend dry, amino-modified motor oligo at 4 mM in ddH2O.
CRITICAL: Benzamide, an oligo synthesis byproduct, can compete with the oligo's amino group for NHS ester reaction and must be removed (Figures 1B and 1C).

Note: We order the motor oligo at a 1 mumol synthesis scale. The resuspension volume of ddH2O is calculated based on the actual oligo yield. For SNAP labeling, we recommend starting with at least 3x molar excess over kinesin dimers; for example, to label 15 nmol kinesin-1 dimers, begin with >= 45 nmol dry oligo.
Pause point: Aliquot desalted motor oligos into 100 muL portions for storage at -80 C.
Aliquot excess BG-GLA-NHS into 10 muL portions, flash freeze, and store at -80 C.
Dissolve 2 mg BG-GLA-NHS in 50 muL anhydrous DMSO to a final concentration of 40 mg/mL (83 mM).

CRITICAL: NHS esters are moisture sensitive. For optimal labelling efficiency, open a new vial of BG-GLA-NHS on the day of the reaction and prepare aliquots immediately to minimize exposure to ambient humidity. Although the manufacturer advises against storing BG-GLA-NHS solubilized in DMSO, we have observed no detectable loss of activity after storage at -80 C for up to 6 months.
Predilute BG-GLA-NHS in anhydrous DMSO to a concentration that is 20x the molar concentration of the desalted motor oligo.
Mix the prediluted BG-GLA-NHS and the motor oligo in equal volumes.
Mix the desalted motor oligo with a 20x molar excess of BG-GLA-NHS in 100 mM sodium borate containing 50% (v/v) DMSO. Incubate at 21 C for 30 min.

Note: Set the total reaction volume to 400-500 muL to match the loading capacity of the PD MiniTrap G-25 gravity column (0.1-0.5 mL) used in the subsequent step. For example, combine 200 muL of 300 muM oligo (in 200 mM sodium borate) with 200 muL of 6 mM BG-GLA-NHS (in DMSO).
Note: NHS ester hydrolysis and amine reactivity both increase at higher pH. Using excess BG-GLA-NHS at pH 8.5 promotes efficient labeling within a short incubation time.
Use a PD MiniTrap G-25 column following the gravity protocol.
Elute with 1.0 mL buffer, collecting ~50 muL fractions. Measure absorbance at 260 nm for each fraction using a Nanodrop (Figure 1A).
Pool fractions corresponding to the first peak, which contains the BG-conjugated oligo.
Determine the concentration of the pooled BG-oligo using a Nanodrop.
Desalt the reaction mixture into 1x PBS containing 1 mM DTT and 1 mM MgCl2 to remove excess BG-GLA-NHS.
Note: The second peak corresponds to NHS released from both hydrolysis and conjugation of BG-GLA-NHS, which strongly absorbs at 260-280 nm.
Run pre- and post-labeling oligos on a 10% TBE-Urea gel. Load 30-50 ng per well and stain with SYBR Green I (Figure 1C). Troubleshooting 1.
Pause point: Store BG-oligo at -20 C and use within 3 days. Longer-term stability has not been tested.

(A) Absorbance at 260 nm of fractions collected during desalting of BG-conjugated oligo.

(B and C) Representative 10% TBE-Urea gel images showing oligo before (pre) and after (post) reaction with BG-GLA-NHS. (B) Incomplete labeling due to high benzamide contamination. (C) Efficient labeling following benzamide removal by desalting.

BG-GLA-NHS is used to link a SNAP-tagged kinesin motor to a DNA oligonucleotide (oligo). The NHS ester reacts with the 5'-end amino group on the DNA oligo to form a stable amide bond. Successful conjugation is confirmed by gel electrophoresis (Figure 1).
Conjugation of BG-oligo to SNAP-tagged kinesin motors
Timing: 1 day
Note: We typically use bacterial pellets from 800 mL cultures and purify on a 1 mL Ni resin gravity column.

Elute the motor protein with 5 mL Elution Buffer containing 1 mM ATP and 1 mM DTT. Monitor GFP fluorescence along the column and begin collecting fractions when a tight, bright green band reaches the bottom.
Note: Our typical yield ~650 muL at ~25 muM.
Pool visibly green fractions. Determine motor concentration by measuring GFP absorbance at 488 nm using a spectrophotometer.
CRITICAL: Perform protein purification and labeling on the same day. SNAP-tag labeling efficiency drops significantly after freezing.
CRITICAL: Include 1 mM DTT or another reducing agent (e.g., beta-mercaptoethanol) in purification and storage buffers to maintain SNAP-tag stability and reactivity.
CRITICAL: Avoid EDTA or other chelating agents, which disrupt the structural Zn2+ ion in the SNAP-tag.
Flash-freeze a few 5 muL aliquots and store at -80 C for future gel analysis.
Purify bacterially expressed kinesin-1, K406GFP-SNAP-His, using Ni-affinity chromatography as described in Uppalapati et al.
Mix BG-oligo and K406GFP-SNAP (dimer) at a 1.5:1 molar ratio. For example, combine 600 muL of K406GFP-SNAP (25 muM dimer) with 375 muL of BG-oligo (60 muM, ~100% labeled). Incubate on ice for 1 h.
Note: Empirically determine the optimal mixing ratio to achieve predominantly single-oligo labeling per motor dimer. Perform small-scale test reaction if needed.
Equilibrate 0.5 mL Ni resin by briefly pulsing in a bench-top centrifuge and resuspending in 0.5 mL Wash Buffer. Repeat two additional times.
Transfer the equilibrated resin to a 0.5 x 10 cm gravity column and allow it to settle.
Dilute the reaction mixture with 1x PBS + 1 mM MgCl2 to reduce the imidazole concentration from the Elution Buffer to ~70 mM. Save 5 muL for gel analysis.
Load the diluted mixture onto the pre-packed Ni column. Collect and save the flow through for gel analysis.
Wash the column with 10 mL Wash Buffer.

Elute K406GFP-SNAP-oligo with 2.5 mL Elution Buffer containing 10 muM ATP and 1 mM DTT. Monitor GFP fluorescence along the column and begin collecting fractions when a tight, bright green band reaches the bottom.
Pool the visibly green fractions and add 1/5 volume of 50% sucrose (final 10%). Determine motor concentration by measuring GFP absorbance at 488 nm using a spectrophotometer.
Purify K406GFP-SNAP-oligo using a pre-packed Ni gravity column.
Note: Our typical yield is ~600 muL at ~10-15 muM.

CRITICAL: Use Ni-affinity chromatography - not desalting - to separate labeled motor from excess BG-oligo for two reasons: (1) The oligo (~20.5 kDa) is not effectively separated from K406GFP-SNAP-His (~114 kDa) by standard desalting columns; (2) Oligo labeling introduces steric hinderance near the His-tag (adjacent to the SNAP-tag), which reduces resin binding by doubly labeled motors - effectively enriching for singly labeled motors (Figures 2A and 2B).

Note: For gravity column purification, pre-pack the resin before sample loading. Avoid incubating the sample with loose resin, which increases the likelihood of 2-oligo populations binding to the resin.
Pause point: Aliquot labeled motors into 5-10 muL portions, flash-freeze, and store at -80 C for up to 6 months.

SDS-PAGE shows increasing molecular weight of K406GFP-SNAP-oligo upon annealing with a clustering oligo containing three complementary binding sites. Lanes 2-5 show samples incubated with increasing concentrations of clustering oligo. At low clustering oligo concentration (lane 2), the labeled motors are predominantly incorporated into fully assembled complexes containing three motors. (A) Coverslips submerged in heated detergent solution on a hot plate during cleaning.
(B) Silanization in a vacuum desiccator; the black dashed line marks the coverslip used to hold the silane, and the yellow arrow indicates the silane location.

Anneal K406GFP-SNAP-oligo with the multivalent clustering oligo and analyze the formation of higher-order motor complexes by SDS-PAGE. Motor clustering increases the molecular weight of the complex, resulting in a mobility shift.
Heat the samples at 90 C for 5 min, then incubate at 21 C for 30 min to allow annealing.
Load the samples onto a 6% Tris-glycine gel and run under denaturing conditions at 100 V on ice or in a 4 C cold room.
Note: Use a low-percentage gel to resolve high-molecular-weight complexes effectively.
Stain the gel using a preferred method (e.g., Coomassie, silver stain) and image. Troubleshooting 3.

Note: Binding of K406GFP-SNAP-oligo to the clustering oligo results in increased molecular weight. The distribution of complexes depends on the ratio of clustering oligo to K406GFP-SNAP-oligo: at lower clustering oligo concentrations, most labeled motors are incorporated into fully assembled clusters (Figure 3, lane 2); as the clustering oligo concentration increases, the proportion of partially assembled complexes containing one or two motors increases (Figure 3, lanes 3-5).

Note: Annealing is inefficient at the low concentrations used in clustering experiments. In our setup, complete clustering is achieved with an approximately 1:1 ratio of labeled motor monomers to clustering oligo. In the example shown in Figure 3, ~10% of K406GFP-SNAP dimers were labeled with a single oligo (determined by native PAGE), corresponding to 5% of total monomers. Of the 30 fmol of total monomers loaded, ~1.5 fmol carried a BG-oligo. To fully cluster the labeled motors, 2 fmol of clustering oligo was required.

Note: Clusters containing one or two motors appear as multiple bands on the gel, which we interpret as reflecting distinct conformations arising from occupation of different clustering-oligo binding sites. Occupation of a single clustering position yields distinct conformations depending on the site occupied, whereas occupation of two positions results in two predominant conformations: side-side (positions 1 and 3) or middle-side (positions 1 and 2 or 2 and 3).
Silanization of coverslips
Timing: 1 day
CRITICAL: Do not substitute the 7x cleaning solution with other detergents. This protocol specifically requires 7x cleaning solution (MP Biomedicals Cat# 097667093).
Prepare a 1:7 dilution of 7x cleaning solution in ddH2O in a deep glass dish or beaker.
Note: The solution appears cloudy at ~20 C and becomes clear upon heating.
Place coverslips on ceramic racks and fully submerge them in the cleaning solution.
Place the dish/beaker on a hot plate set to 450 C. Heat until the solution becomes clear but does not boil; adjust the temperature if necessary (Figure 4A).
Maintain heating for 2 h. Add ddH2O as needed to keep coverslips fully submerged.
Clean coverslips.
Remove coverslips from the cleaning solution and rinse thoroughly with ddH2O.
Note: Properly cleaned coverslips should be hydrophilic at this stage; water should spread evenly across the surface.
Dry the coverslips thoroughly using clean nitrogen gas.
Treat the racked coverslips in a plasma cleaner at high RF level for 12 min.
Place the racked coverslips into a vacuum desiccator.
Place one clean coverslip in the center of the desiccator to hold the silane.
Add 100 muL of 1H,1H,2H,2H-Perfluorodecyltrichlorosilane onto the central coverslip.
Immediately close the desiccator and gently evacuate.
Silanize coverslips (Figure 4B).
CRITICAL: Silane is highly moisture sensitive. Add the silane quickly and seal the desiccator immediately to minimize exposure to ambient humidity.
After 16-20 h, remove coverslips from the desiccator and store in a clean box.
CRITICAL: Verify successful silanization by placing a drop of water on a coverslip; the contact angle should exceed 90  on a well-silanized surface (Figure 4C).
Preparation of liposomes
Timing: ~6 h
Dissolve individual lipid components in chloroform and store at -20 C until use.
Prepare the lipid mixture by combining POPC, DSPE-PEG(2000)-Biotin, and Atto 647N DOPE in chloroform at a 99:1:0.05 molar ratio, with a total lipid concentration of 10 mg/mL.

In this step, lipids are combined in the desired molar ratio in chloroform, dried to form a thin film, and rehydrated with buffer to generate multilamellar vesicles. These vesicles are then subjected to freeze-thaw cycles to reduce size and lamellarity, followed by extrusion through membrane filters to yield liposomes with a narrow size distribution.
Note: Use only glass syringes, pipettes, and containers when handling chloroform. Perform all steps involving chloroform inside a fume hood.
After the bulk solvent has evaporated (~1.5 h for 500 muL), continue drying under vacuum in the evaporator for an additional 3 h to remove residual chloroform.
Evaporate the chloroform using a rotary evaporator at 450 mmHg and 260 rpm.
Alternatives: If a rotary evaporator is unavailable, dry the chloroform under a gentle stream of nitrogen gas and then place the lipid film under vacuum for 3 h.
Rehydrate the dried lipid film in 500 muL BRB80 to achieve a final lipid concentration of 10 mg/mL.
Incubate at 21 C for 30 min, vortexing periodically to create a uniform suspension.
Note: The resulting solution will contain multilamellar vesicles and should appear cloudy at this stage.
Subject the lipid suspension to 10 freeze-thaw cycles by alternating between liquid nitrogen and a warm water bath (~40 C).
Note: The suspension will appear less cloudy after this step, reflecting decreased lamellarity and vesicle size.

Pause point: Prior to the last freeze-thaw cycle, the lipid suspension can be aliquoted (100 muL each), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, and store at -80 C for 1-2 months. We avoid using them after 2 months due to potential lipid oxidation.
Assemble the mini-extruder and extrude the lipid suspension 21 times through two stacked 100-nm polycarbonate membrane filters.
Note: The liposome solution should appear clear after extrusion. Dynamic light scattering (DLS) measurements typically show a mean diameter of ~120 nm (Figure 5).
Note: Refer to Avanti's guidelines for mini-extruder assembly and extrusion technique: https://avantiresearch.com/products/equipment/category/mini-extruder.
Pause point: Store liposomes at 4 C for up to a week.

Note: The K406GFP-SNAP construct tends to express as inclusion bodies under our standard bacterial expression protocol. Since the T7 system is strong and not tunable, reducing IPTG concentration is not effective for lowering expression. To mitigate this, we use Tuner(DE3) cells, a BL21 derivative with a lacY (encoding lac permease) mutation that enables uniform and concentration-dependent IPTG uptake. This lowers intracellular IPTG levels and slows protein expression. By inducing at higher OD and expressing at low levels over a prolonged period, sufficient soluble protein can be obtained. We typically induce cultures in Terrific Broth with 0.6 mM IPTG at OD600 ~2.5 and express for ~20 h at 21 C. This strategy may be useful for other proteins prone to forming inclusion bodies.

Alternatives: This protein engineering approach can be adapted to other cytoskeletal motors with minor modifications. Two design principles are essential: (1) the motor must be in an active, non-autoinhibited state (e.g., truncated kinesin-1 lacking the tail domain, or mammalian dynein complexed with dynactin and an activating cargo adaptor); and (2) the motor must carry a tag that enables covalent attachment of a DNA oligo (SNAP tag in this protocol, or HaloTag as described in). As an alternative to GFP fusion, SNAP tags not occupied by DNA oligos can be labeled with a fluorescent dye (e.g., BG-Alexa Fluor 488) by adding a 10-fold molar excess of dye after oligo labeling in step 7 in before you begin and incubating for 15 min at 4 C, as described in. Regardless of whether fluorescence is provided by GFP or a dye, it is critical to maintain a low oligo labeling fraction (~10-15%) to avoid motors carrying two oligos. If higher labeling efficiency is required, heterodimeric motors in which only one monomer carries a SNAP tag can be expressed and purified, as described in.

Bacterial pellets containing dual-labeled motor proteins: We use a truncated kinesin-1 construct (K406GFP-SNAP), comprising the first 406 amino acids of Drosophila kinesin heavy chain fused to eGFP, a SNAP-tag, and a C-terminal 6xHis-tag. The protein is bacterially expressed, and cell pellets are stored at -80 C for up to 3 weeks. Purify the protein on the same day as oligo labeling to preserve SNAP-tag reactivity.
Alternatives: Porcine brain tubulin is commercially available (Cytoskeleton Cat# T240).

Note: We visualize unlabeled microtubules using interference reflection microscopy (IRM) implemented on a custom-built microscope. IRM can also be readily implemented on a standard total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscope with minimal microscope modification. Alternatively, unlabeled microtubules can be visualized by differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy.
80 muM bovine brain tubulin: For detailed preparation, see Uppalapati et al. Tubulin is flash-frozen and stored as 10 muL aliquots at -80 C for up to a year.

16.7 muM NeutrAvidin: Dissolve 10 mg NeutrAvidin in 1 mL of 10% glycerol. Then add 9 mL of BRB80 to achieve a final concentration of 1 mg/mL (16.7 muM). Aliquot into 45 muL portions, flash-freeze, and store at -80 C for up to a year.
Anti-tubulin antibody: Aliquot into 5 muL portions upon receipt. Flash-freeze and store at -80 C for up to a year. Once thawed, an aliquot can be stored at 4 C for a few weeks.

20 mg/mL casein: Prepare 50 mg/mL casein by dissolving 2.5 g casein in 50 mL BRB80. Mix for ~16 h at 4 C. Centrifuge at 20,000 xg, 4 C for 20 min to remove aggregates. Collect the supernatant and ultracentrifuge at 228,200 xg (50,000 rpm with Beckman Coulter Type 50.2 Ti rotor), 4 C for 30 min. Filter through a 0.45 mum filter. Measure concentration by absorbance at 280 nm (extinction coefficient: 1.177 mg/ml-1 cm-1). Adjust to 20 mg/mL with BRB80. Aliquot into 50 muL portions, flash-freeze, and store at -80 C for up to a year.

50 mg/mL BSA: Prepare 100 mg/mL BSA by dissolving 5 g BSA in 50 mL BRB80. Filter through a 0.45 mum filter. Measure concentration by absorbance at 280 nm (extinction coefficient: 43,824 M-1 cm-1; MW: 66,463 Da). Adjust to 50 mg/mL with BRB80. Aliquot into 50 muL portions, flash-freeze, and store at -80 C for up to a year.

CRITICAL: DMSO is hygroscopic, and taxol aliquots may appear partially or fully liquid at -20 C due to water accumulation, which lowers the freezing point. Because taxol is extremely insoluble in water, discard any aliquots that fail to freeze completely.
1 mM taxol: Dissolve 5 mg Paclitaxel in 5.8 mL anhydrous DMSO. Aliquot into 25 muL portions and store at -20 C. Aliquots are stable for 6 months if water does not accumulate.
1 M DTT: Dissolve 308.5 mg DTT in 2 mL ddH2O. Filter through a 0.2 mum filter. Aliquot into 10 muL portions and store at -20 C for up to 6 months.
100 mM MgATP: Dissolve 551.14 mg ATP in 9.5 mL ddH2O. Add 500 muL MgCl2 (2 M) and mix well. Filter through a 0.2 mum filter. Aliquot into 25 muL portions and store at -20 C for up to a year.
50 mM MgAMPPNP: Dissolve 50 mg AMPPNP in 1.95 mL ddH2O. Add 50 muL MgCl2 (2 M) and mix well. Filter through a 0.2 mum filter. Aliquot into 25 muL portions and store at -20 C for up to a year.
25 mM MgGTP: Dissolve 65 mg GTP in 5 mL ddH2O. Add 62.5 muL MgCl2 (2 M) and mix well. Filter through a 0.2 mum filter. Aliquot into 5 muL portions and store at -20 C for up to a year.
2 M D-glucose: Dissolve 3.6 g Dextrose in ddH2O (total volume 10 mL). Filter through a 0.2 mum filter. Aliquot into 25 muL portions and store at -20 C for up to a year.
2 mg/mL glucose oxidase: Dissolve the entire bottle of glucose oxidase (10 KU, 250 U/mg) in 20 mL cold BRB80. Aliquot into 12 muL portions, flash-freeze, and store at -80 C for up to a year.
0.8 mg/mL catalase: Dissolve 16 mg catalase in 20 mL cold BRB80. Aliquot into 12 muL portions, flash-freeze, and store at -80 C for up to a year.
5% (w/v) F-127: Dissolve 50 mg Pluronic F-127 in 1 mL BRB80. Mix overnight to fully dissolve. Centrifuge at 10,000 xg for 10 min and collect the supernatant. Store at ~21 C for up to 2 weeks.

Step-by-step method details
Purification of active kinesin-NeutrAvidin complexes by microtubule pelleting assay
Timing: 1.5 h
Add 0.5 muL DMSO, 0.4 muL MgCl2 (100 mM), and 0.4 muL MgGTP (25 mM) directly to a 10 muL aliquot of tubulin (80 muM) and mix well.
Incubate at 37 C for 35 min.
Polymerize microtubules in BRB80 with 5% (v/v) DMSO, 4 mM MgCl2, and 1 mM MgGTP.
While microtubules are polymerizing, prepare pelleting solutions.
5 min before the microtubules are ready, mix 400 nM K406GFP-SNAP-oligo with 4 muM NeutrAvidin in Pelleting Buffer. Incubate at ~21 C for 5 min.

This procedure purifies active K406GFP-SNAP-oligo-NeutrAvidin by first pelleting motor proteins that can bind microtubules in the presence of a non-hydrolysable ATP analog (AMPPNP). The pellet is then resuspended in ATP to release active motors into the supernatant, while irreversibly bound motors remain in the pellet. This purification is performed on the day of the microscopy experiments to remove motors that have become inactive during expression, purification, or storage.
Note: NeutrAvidin has 4 biotin binding sites, and a 10:1 molar excess of NeutrAvidin is recommended to avoid cross-linking of K406GFP-SNAP-oligo.

Once microtubules are polymerized,
Spin solutions from steps 4.a and 4.b in the Airfuge at 20 psi for 3 min.

Gently resuspend the stabilized microtubule pellet (from step 4.b) with 80 muL of BRB80 + 10 muM taxol. Keep at ~21 C for microscopy experiments.
Discard the supernatant.
Spin the resuspended motor sample at 30 psi for 5 min.
Collect the supernatant, which contains active K406GFP-SNAP-oligo-NeutrAvidin and K406GFP-SNAP. Keep on ice.

Liposome flotation assay

(A) Schematic of liposome flotation assay. Liposome and motor mixture is loaded to the bottom layer of a sucrose gradient. Upon centrifugation, liposomes with the attached motors 'float' to the top layer, while the unattached motors remain at the bottom.
(B) Photograph showing that a high concentration of liposomes containing Atto 647N DOPE accumulates at the top layer after the flotation assay.

(C) Sample distribution post-flotation. Blue squares and green triangles show relative fluorescence signal of liposomes and motors, respectively, when the mixture is loaded to the bottom layer prior to flotation. Gray triangles show motor distribution post flotation when liposomes are omitted. Each data point represents the mean of three independent measurements and for each condition, values are normalized to the maximum value. Error bars indicate SD.

(D) An example of kinesin-1 concentrations in the top 100 muL (green), middle 450 muL (blue), and bottom 450 muL (gray) fractions after the liposome flotation assay at various kinesin-1/liposome mixing ratios. Ratios are varied by changing liposome concentration while keeping kinesin-1 constant, except for the ratio of 100, where kinesin-1 is doubled. Figure is reprinted with permission from Jiang et al., 2025.

K406GFP-SNAP-oligo-NeutrAvidin complexes bind to DSPE-PEG(2000)-Biotin on liposomes. After layering the mixture at the bottom of a sucrose gradient and centrifugation, liposomes with attached motors float to the top, while unbound motors remain at the bottom (Figures 6A-6C). This ensures: 1) The clustering oligo alters the organization of pre-bound motors without recruiting additional motors; 2) excess unlabeled K406GFP-SNAP does not interfere with motor number quantification in the microscopy experiment.

Note: To ensure consistent clustering oligo occupancy across different motor densities on liposomes, the motor concentration in solution is held constant. This is achieved by keeping the volume of motor-NeutrAvidin complexes constant (except at the highest mixing ratio) and varying the liposome volume on a semi-log scale.

Note: Motor copy number per liposome depends on the mixing ratio and varies with oligo labeling efficiency, active motor yield, and liposome counts. Adjust the volumes of liposomes and motor-NeutrAvidin complexes empirically such that ~5 nM motor is recovered from the top fraction in step 18.
Add 200 muL of flotation buffer with 60% sucrose to each sample and mix well to create a 30% sucrose bottom layer (Figure 6A).
Tilt the tube at 45  and carefully overlay 25% sucrose buffer using a 500 muL point-tip Hamilton syringe (Cat# 80800).
Add 100 muL flotation buffer (no sucrose) as the top layer using a 100 muL Hamilton syringe.
Centrifuge at 174,636 xg (45,000 rpm with Type 50.2 Ti rotor), 4 C, for 45 min.
Note: For fixed-angle rotors (e.g., Type 50.2 Ti), maximum acceleration/deceleration is fine. For swinging-bucket rotors, use slow ramps to avoid disturbing layers.
Remove tubes carefully and keep on ice. High-concentration Atto 647N-labeled liposomes may appear as a blue rim in the top layer (Figure 6B).
Use a flat-tip 500 muL Hamilton syringe (Cat# 80865) to fractionate from the bottom: collect 450 muL bottom, 450 muL middle, and 100 muL top fractions.

Measure GFP and Atto 647N fluorescence in each fraction using a plate reader. Use a GFP calibration curve to quantify motor concentration (Figures 6C and 6D) (see expected outcomes). Troubleshooting 4 and 5.
CRITICAL: For subsequent experiments, we target recovery of ~5 nM motor in the top fraction at this step.
Save the top fractions containing liposomes with bound motors. Keep on ice.
Prepare 100 nM Cy3-clustering oligo by diluting the 100 muM stock 1:1,000 in BRB80.
Add 1 muL of 100 nM Cy3-clustering oligo to each 20 muL sample.
Take 20 muL of each top fraction and incubate with 5 nM Cy3-clustering oligo on ice for 30 min to induce clustering.
Motor number quantification by GFP fluorescence
Timing: 30 min per sample
Make a flow cell by sandwiching two strips of double-sided tape (~2 mm apart) between a silanized coverslip and a glass slide (Figure 7).
Note: Narrow flow cells minimize sample volume, improve solution exchange efficiency, and increase flow rate to facilitate microtubule alignment.
Flow in 5 muL anti-tubulin antibody (1:50 in BRB80); incubate 5 min.
Wash with 20 muL BRB80.
Flow in 20 muL 5% F-127; incubate 5 min.

Expected outcomes

Expected outcome for liposome flotation assay: liposomes with bound motors float to the top, and unbound motors remain at the bottom (Figures 6B and 6C). With constant motor input and varying liposome concentrations, motor concentrations in the top fraction remain similar across different mixing ratios (Figure 6D).
Example kymographs showing liposomes travel for longer distances when the motors are clustered (cyan arrow heads) compared to when the motors are unclustered (magenta arrow heads)

Expected liposome motility: Liposomes move along microtubules at velocities similar to or slightly below the single-molecule speed of kinesin-1 (500-600 nm/s). Average travel distance increases with motor number. At low to moderate motor densities (<15 motors per liposome), clustering markedly extends run length (Figure 9), whereas at high motor densities, clustering does not measurably affect run length.
Quantification and statistical analysis

Motor number on liposomes was measured by ratio-metric comparison of GFP fluorescence from K406GFP-SNAP in AMPPMP. The details were described in. Briefly, the fluorescence intensity of individual K406GFP-SNAP molecules is measured and fitted with a sum of two normal distributions, corresponding to motors carrying one or two fluorescent GFPs. This calibration is used to estimate the probability of a GFP molecule being fluorescent and to derive the expected GFP intensity distribution for liposomes bearing defined numbers of motors, while accounting for the measured liposome size distribution. Motor number per liposome is then determined by comparing the experimentally measured GFP intensity distribution of liposomes to the predicted distributions.
Liposome and single-K406GFP-SNAP motility was analyzed by kymographs using Fiji.
Limitations

This system is designed to achieve stable motor clustering (expected lifetime on the order of 105 s) during individual liposome runs (<=16 s). However, clustering dynamics mediated by scaffolding proteins in vivo may be considerably more transient.

Because motor attachment to liposomes is stochastic, average motor number scales only approximately with the motor-to-liposome mixing ratio, making precise control of motor loading difficult. Therefore, conclusions drawn solely from mixing ratios can be misleading - it is essential to group data based on experimentally measured motor numbers determined from fluorescence intensity.

Furthermore, the combination of stochastic motor loading and the lognormal distribution of liposome sizes produces overlapping motor number distributions between motor densities. This overlap can obscure subtle effects of clustering. Since liposomes with higher motor copy numbers have an increased likelihood of recruiting clustering oligos, comparisons between unclustered and clustered conditions must be made using the experimentally measured motor densities rather than nominal mixing ratios.
Troubleshooting
Problem 1
Only a small fraction of oligos are labeled with BG-GLA-NHS, even when a large excess of BG-GLA-NHS is used (related to step 5 in before you begin).
Potential solution

This issue is likely caused by benzamide contamination from the oligo synthesis, which competes with the amino-modified oligo for reacting with the NHS ester. Desalt the oligo thoroughly before the labeling reaction to remove benzamide and other small-molecule contaminants.
Problem 2
Oligo labeling efficiency of SNAP-tagged motors is low (related to step 9 in before you begin).
Potential solution

This issue is likely caused by reduced SNAP-tag activity. Purify the motors on the same day as oligo labeling and avoid any freeze-thaw cycles prior to labeling. Include a reducing agent (e.g., DTT, beta-mercaptoethanol) in the motor buffer and ensure that chelating agents such as EDTA are absent, as the SNAP-tag contains a structural Zn2+ ion.
Problem 3
Failure to observe a shift to higher molecular weight in EMSA (related to step 13 in before you begin).
Potential solution
The complementary sequence in the clustering region may have a low melting temperature (Tm). Increase the length or GC content of the clustering sequence to achieve a Tm above 50 C.
Excessive heat buildup during electrophoresis may cause oligo detachment. Use chilled running buffer, run the gel at a lower voltage, and perform electrophoresis in a cold environment.
The ionic strength of the sample buffer may be too high. Prepare the 2x EMSA sample buffer according to the recipe provided in this protocol.
Gel percentage may be too high. Use a low-percentage gel to resolve high-molecular-weight complexes effectively.
Problem 4
Motors do not bind to liposomes (related to step 18).
Potential solution

Verify that both the motor oligo and liposomes contain biotin. Biotin concentration can be measured using a commercial kit (e.g., Thermo Scientific Cat# 46610). This assay may need to be performed on the motor oligo prior to conjugation, as only a small fraction of motors carry oligo and the resulting biotin concentration may fall below the detection limit.
Confirm that NeutrAvidin is present and functional.

Check that the motor oligo is attached and intact by SDS-PAGE (showing a shift to the expected higher molecular weight). If degradation is observed, ensure all reagents and consumables are DNase-free and prepare a fresh batch of motor oligo and oligo-labeled motors.
Problem 5
Incorrect sample distribution after the liposome flotation assay (related to step 18).
Potential solution
Ensure all buffers are pre-chilled before layering the sucrose gradient. After centrifugation, keep tubes on ice until fractionation.

When overlaying a new layer, tilt the tube ~45 , place the needle tip against the tube wall just above the previous layer, and slowly release the solution to avoid mixing. Once all layers are added, gently return the tube to an upright position.
Handle tubes carefully when transferring between the ultracentrifuge and the bench to prevent disturbing the gradient.

Use a syringe with a flat-tip needle for fractionation. Drawing fractions from the bottom with a needle yields more consistent and reproducible results than pipetting from the top. The flat tip ensures no gap between the needle and the tube bottom. Insert and withdraw the needle vertically and steadily to minimize layer disturbance.

Clean the syringe with buffer between samples. It is not necessary to rinse the needle between collecting the bottom and middle layers of the same sample (these layers are discarded), but use a Kimwipe to remove excess liquid before re-inserting the needle.
Collect the top layer using a micropipette with a clean tip.
Problem 6
No colocalization between clustering oligo and liposomes (related to steps 30 and 34).
Potential solution
Verify the integrity of the clustering oligo by running it on a 10% TBE-Urea gel.
Confirm that both the clustering and motor oligos have the correct sequences, and validate motor cluster formation by EMSA.
Increase the concentration of clustering oligo added to the liposomes to improve binding efficiency.
Problem 7
Clustering oligo does not improve liposome travel distances (related to step 34).
Potential solution

Inconsistent results often arise when data are not analyzed based on the experimentally measured motor number or when clustering oligo incorporation is not confirmed. To ensure accurate interpretation, map all data according to the measured motor number (from GFP fluorescence), and classify only Cy3+ liposomes as those transported by clustered motors.

passages.text: Scalable Ru-Doped Pt/NiFe-LDH Catalyst via Pulse Electrolysis Enables Stable Glycerol Oxidation to Glyceric Acid at High Current Density.

Selective electrooxidation of glycerol (GLY) to glyceric acid (GLA) offers a promising route for GLY valorization but remains hindered by limited activity and stability. Herein, we report a scalable self-corrosion strategy for large-area fabrication of a Ru-doped Pt/NiFe-LDH catalyst on Ni foam (PtRu/NiFe-LDH) with an area of up to 36 cm2. The incorporation of Ru modulates the electronic structure, enhances the adsorption of both OH- and GLY, and lowers the free energy barrier for OH* formation, thereby significantly boosting catalytic activity to achieve a recorded current density of 439.5 mA cm- 2. Furthermore, pulse electrolysis effectively suppresses the formation of PtOx, ensuring long-term stability. When integrated into a GLY oxidation-assisted hydrogen evolution system, this bifunctional catalyst reduces the cell voltage by 1.01 V relative to conventional water splitting, while delivering 78.5% selectivity towards GLA and stable operation for over 120 h. This work establishes a viable pathway toward the industrialization of selective electrochemical oxidation of GLY to GLA by integrating advanced catalyst design with optimized electrolyzer configuration.

passages.text: A combined TLC-GC approach for the regiospecific analysis of triacylglycerols in Yarrowia lipolytica.

This study developed a robust, cost-effective thin-layer chromatography (TLC) combined with gas chromatography (GC) protocol for the regiospecific analysis of triacylglycerols (TAGs), with application to microbial oils from engineered Yarrowia lipolytica. Key steps, such as sn-1,3-specific lipase hydrolysis, TLC separation, staining, and fatty acid methyl ester (FAME) derivatization, were systematically optimized. Porcine pancreatic lipase was identified as the most efficient and economical enzyme for hydrolysis. A petroleum ether/diethyl ether/acetic acid (32:8:0.8, v/v/v) TLC solvent system provided optimal resolution, with iodine vapor as the preferred non-destructive staining method. BF3-methanol methylation prevented artifact formation observed with methanol-H2SO4. Applied to oils from strains producing nervonic acid (NA) and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), the method revealed distinct regiospecific patterns: NA was almost exclusively esterified at the sn-1,3 positions, whereas approximately 64.3% of GLA resided at the sn-2 position. This TLC-GC approach offers an accessible alternative for rapid screening of fatty acid positional distribution in TAGs.

passages.text: Mouse models of tuberculosis uniformly featuring hypoxic necrotic lesions and poor response to chemotherapy.

Mouse models have been key to studies of tuberculosis pathogenesis and drug efficacy, but many, such as those employing BALB/c mice, fail to reproduce the full range of heterogenous microniches observed in well-structured human lesions, which feature hypoxic caseous cores of necrotic debris surrounded by infected foamy macrophages. The granuloma presents a variety of environments differing in levels of oxygen, ions, nutrients, and intra versus extracellular residence, which determine the physiological state of the infecting bacillus and its susceptibility to immune or drug control. Recently, alternative mouse strains such as C3HeB/FeJ have allowed the study of infection and treatment in the context of these varied environments but exhibit substantial inconsistency in the development of hypoxic necrotic lesions, both within and between individual mice. Building on the observation that inducible nitric oxide synthase (Nos2)-deficient mice consistently develop hypoxic necrotic lesions, we have established two simplified models with infection by the aerosol route. The first uses the slightly attenuated M. tuberculosis R1Rv strain, which produces a progressive infection that is contained at a high stable burden by an adaptive immune response. In the second model, vaccination with the attenuated  RD1, pantothenate auxotroph mc26230 protects from an otherwise lethal infection with virulent Mycobacterium tuberculosis Erdman. This model reflects most contemporary tuberculosis infections, which take place in the context of a pre-existing immune response from vaccination. Both variations uniformly develop well-structured hypoxic necrotic lesions and respond poorly to chemotherapy. These refined models will be useful in studies of M. tuberculosis infection and treatment.

passages.text: Significant Correlation Between White Matter Hyperintensity Volume and Rare NOTCH3 Variants in the General Japanese Population.

AIM: Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD)-related MRI findings, including white matter hyperintensities (WMHs), are not rare in general elderly populations. The aim of this study was to elucidate the contribution of hereditary CSVD-related genes to CSVD-related MRI findings in a general Japanese population. METHODS: We analyzed datasets from 324 individuals aged >= 50 years in Tohoku Medical Megabank (TMM), focusing on MRI markers and variants of NOTCH3, ABCC6, COL4A1, COL4A2, GLA, HTRA1, and TREX1 genes. Background factors included age, sex, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, hyperuricemia, alcohol drinking, and smoking. RESULTS: Pathogenic variant carriers were identified within ABCC6 (n = 20), but not other genes. To compare with previous studies including rare NOTCH3 variants regardless of pathogenicity, we included 24 rare functional variants of NOTCH3. We performed a gene-based analysis using the burden test and sequence kernel association test (SKAT) adjusted for background factors, between WMH/lacune and ABCC6/NOTCH3. The only significant finding was the correlation between WMH volume and rare NOTCH3 variants by SKAT, both with the basic model, adjusted for age, sex, and hypertension (p = 0.045), and full model, adjusted for all background factors (p = 0.027). We also analyzed the association between intracranial major artery stenosis/occlusion (ICASO) and RNF213 p.Arg4810Lys, the East Asian-specific variant susceptible to ICASO; however, we failed to identify a significant correlation. CONCLUSIONS: This study suggests that NOTCH3 may contribute to WMH volume in a general Japanese population.
Lipid metabolism classification of gliomas.

Lipid metabolic reprogramming represents a fundamental oncogenic mechanism. However, clinical relevance of lipid metabolism (LM) alterations in gliomas remain to be fully elucidated. LM-based classification and subsequent correlative analyses were performed using glioma bulk RNA-seq datasets retrieved from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). Radiomic models were constructed and validated using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) datasets from The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) and our in-house glioma cohort. Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining was employed to detect the protein expression of the key gene in glioma tissue samples. Single cell RNA-seq datasets from the GBMap database were used to characterize the distribution and functional roles of the key gene in the tumor microenvironment (TME) of gliomas. Consensus clustering based on LM pathways identified three distinct subtypes, respectively dominated by steroid metabolism (ST-type), triglyceride metabolism (TC-type), and sphingolipid metabolism (SP-type). The SP-type was independently associated with poorer prognosis and displayed enhanced activity in pathways linked to aggressive tumor phenotypes and radiotherapy resistance. Radiomic features enabled accurate identification of SP-type gliomas, thereby offering a non-invasive strategy for predicting this subtype. Genes GLA, GBL1, and HSD3B7 were identified as signature genes of the SP-type. Higher expression of HSD3B7 was associated with poor prognosis and exerted functional effects on multiple signaling pathways across various cellular components of the TME, which may contribute to glioma progression. Gliomas exhibited marked heterogeneity in LM and can be classified into three subtypes, with the SP-type exhibiting the most aggressive clinical behavior.

passages.text: Case Series: Use of Dalbavancin for Invasive Gram-Positive Infection in Children.

OBJECTIVE: Dalbavancin, a lipoglycopeptide antibiotic active against Gram-positive bacteria with a prolonged in vivo half-life, was recently approved by the Food and Drug Administration for use in pediatric skin/soft tissue infection. Although use in adult skin/soft tissue infection and off-label use in adult osteoarticular and bloodstream infection are well documented, pediatric data are limited to pharmacokinetic data, 1 clinical trial, and case reports/series. Here, we describe the clinical and microbiologic details of cases in which dalbavancin was used at 2 pediatric hospitals. METHODS: Chart review of all patients receiving dalbavancin for any indication in 2 pediatric hospitals between August 2020 and July 2025. RESULTS: Dalbavancin was used in 20 patients (age range 2 weeks to 18 years) in the time period. Fifteen cases had infection with either methicillin-susceptible or -resistant Staphylococcus aureus, 16 had bacteremia, 2 had endocarditis, and 11 cases had isolates available for dalbavancin susceptibility testing; all proved susceptible. Reasons for dalbavancin use included need for intravenous therapy with relative contraindications for alternative oral antibiotics or outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy, difficulty of intravenous access, and medication nonadherence. Most cases had an uncomplicated recovery. None had microbiologic failure. CONCLUSIONS: With the limitations of this series and prior published data, dalbavancin may be a safe and efficacious antibiotic for use in certain invasive Gram-positive infections in children. It is a reasonable alternative when faced with relative contraindications to inpatient or outpatient parenteral therapy, especially when bactericidal therapy is needed or preferred. Formal pediatric trials against the standard of care, especially beyond skin/soft tissue infection, are encouraged.

passages.text: Identification and validation of gamma-Linolenic acid as a natural FABP5 inhibitor in hepatocellular carcinoma through deep learning and experimental approaches.

Background: Fatty acid binding protein 5 (FABP5) is implicated in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression and represents a potential therapeutic target. Methods: We integrated machine learning-based virtual screening, molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations to identify natural compounds with high binding affinity to FABP5. Candidate compounds were further validated by in-vitro assays in HCC cell lines, including proliferation, migration/invasion, apoptosis/ferroptosis-related readouts, and mechanistic validation. Results: The optimized models enabled efficient screening of natural products and prioritized gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) as a top candidate FABP5 inhibitor. Docking and simulations supported stable binding and key residue interactions. Experimentally, GLA inhibited HCC cell proliferation and aggressiveness and promoted cell death-related pathways consistent with anti-tumor activity. Conclusion: Our deep learning-guided workflow identified gamma-linolenic acid as a natural FABP5 inhibitor and supports its potential as a lead compound for HCC therapy.
